articles.title_orig: Two Iranians charged over alleged plot targeting Jewish community in UK
articles.title_zh: Two Iranians charged over alleged plot targeting Jewish community in UK
articles.content_orig:
British authorities have charged two Iranian nationals with planning an attack against the Jewish community in northern England.
The UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said on Friday that Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with “preparing to commit or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism” in Manchester “on or before” Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, which began at sundown on September 20.
“It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot,” police said in a separate statement on Friday.
Details of the alleged plot have not been released, but police have confirmed its “disruption”.
Counterterrorism police said Salehi and Ahmadyan, both arrested in Manchester on September 20, allegedly tried to acquire components and equipment to make an improvised explosive device and conducted reconnaissance on potential targets for attack.
The pair will appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Saturday, the CPS said.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Salehi and Ahmadyan arrived in the UK on a small boat from Europe several years ago. One of the men had been granted asylum and the other had a live asylum claim, the Home Office said.
“It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime,” she said in a statement.
“They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement,” she added.
Iran has denied similar accusations.
The charges come a year after two people were killed in a knife and gun attack by a British citizen of Syrian descent at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in northern Manchester on October 2, 2025.
“I’m aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy day period has caused a great deal of concern to the Jewish community, as well as with the wider public,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said on Friday.
“It also coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the UK.”
Detectives said there was no connection between Friday’s charges and the suspected plot involving the RAF Fairford air base, over which a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on Thursday, according to the Reuters news agency.
Britain said Tehran had been involved in an alleged plot earlier this week targeting an airbase used by the US to launch attacks against Iran.
Iran denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford plot and said speculation would “fuel Iranophobia propaganda”.

articles.title_orig: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc
articles.title_zh: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc
articles.content_orig:
Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election
S hortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.
“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.
Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.
On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.
Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.
Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro , 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.
“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum , is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.
“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.
Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs ” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land .
While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.
Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth , but it is currently at a low point , with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.
“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”
A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.
At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.
Privileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals was one of the conditions Washington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has offered those natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.
“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup to overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.
“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.
As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.
Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he took fourth place in Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – some shelved , others still under investigation – has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.
Unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen , and average incomes have risen, but so has household debt – something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated and Lula banned days before the vote.
The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving supreme court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.
Many therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from a simple transfer of his father’s voter base and from an anti-Lula vote .
“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.
Actor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed by Jair Bolsonaro’s election that she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.
She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.
She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.
“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.

articles.title_orig: Chinese lithium mine registers wider vein, bolstering Beijing’s battery supply
articles.title_zh: Chinese lithium mine registers wider vein, bolstering Beijing’s battery supply
articles.content_orig:
A deposit in Sichuan has registered over 1 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, adding to China’s stores of the valuable metal
China has announced the expansion of the resource base for a major lithium deposit in the southwestern province of Sichuan by about 70 per cent, strengthening the country’s potential long-term supply for the metal – an essential component in the production of batteries for electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage.
After recent detection efforts, the Jiada Lithium Mine has registered about 1.05 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent in the deposit, bringing its total resources to 2.53 million tonnes, state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday. The increase reinforces the mine’s status as a major hard-rock lithium deposit.
Dazhong Mining, the project’s developer, said in a filing that the additional resources had passed review and registration by the Ministry of Natural Resources. They comprise 33.52 million tonnes of ore containing about 423,800 tonnes of lithium oxide, with an average grade of 1.26 per cent.
The addition represents a 70.5 per cent increase from the previously registered 1.48 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, according to the filing.

articles.title_orig: Manchester Half Marathon: Dad with MS attempts world record
articles.title_zh: Manchester Half Marathon: Dad with MS attempts world record
articles.content_orig:
A man from Liverpool has set himself the challenge of breaking a Guinness World Record for the fastest half marathon run by a man with multiple sclerosis (MS).
Father-of-two David Price, 42, was diagnosed with MS in 2018 after starting to struggle with his balance and peripheral vision.
Eight years on, Price is preparing to attempt the record at the Manchester Half Marathon, but admits to feeling nervous.
The current record is held by Chris White, who achieved a time of 1 hour 30 minutes and 46 seconds in Brighton in March this year.
"It would mean the world to me to break the record," David said. "I'm not underestimating how much of a challenge it will be, but it would be absolutely fantastic."
David, who works in IT, said his symptoms of MS first became noticeable in the office.
"I was stumbling around the office and knocking things off desks. My peripheral vision and senses had gone a little bit strange and weird," he said, adding that he also "started to get tingling arms and legs."
David described his diagnosis of MS as a "shock to the system", and something that took a long time to come to terms with.
"Me and the wife didn't have a clue what multiple sclerosis was," David recalled.
"It took me about three years to accept I had this long-term disability."
Despite medication, life has its daily challenges.
"You will have times where your cognitive functions aren't quite right or your thought process isn't quite where it should be.
"Like when you try to speak. You know what you want to say, but you struggle to get it out."
In 2021, David started to run and lift weights, something he said brought out a "remarkable" change in him.
"I never looked back from that point," he said. "I changed my mindset."
Training for Sunday's race, David said he has been listening to his body closely.
"I've got to accept that just because it's on the training plan, doesn't mean it has to be done.
"I've got to be big enough to say I'm not capable of doing that today - I need to take a rest day.'"
He said he wanted to attempt the world record to show others that setting high goals is possible.
"I'm not defined by MS," he said.
"And MS doesn't define me."
The Manchester Half Marathon takes place on Sunday 4 October.

articles.title_orig: America’s data center fight is a preview of what's to come for the rest of the world
articles.title_zh: America’s data center fight is a preview of what's to come for the rest of the world
articles.content_orig:
As the AI boom becomes a major part of political debate, the public backlash against data centers in the U.S. is spreading to Europe and Asia — raising risks for investors.
Across the Atlantic, negative sentiment is growing in Europe, which has more at stake due to its densely populated countries and higher electricity prices , experts told CNBC.
Similar tensions are emerging in South Korea, with growing opposition to data centers near residential areas and proposals for tighter local restrictions, even as the national government pushes to accelerate development.
Public opposition has already impacted around $42 billion of data center investments in Europe, in account delays and cancellations, according to research from STL Partners. That compares to around $77 billion in the U.S.
The pushback could be the "straw that breaks the camel's back," Olivier Darmouni, associate professor at HEC Paris who specializes in the energy transition, told CNBC.
More than 70 data center projects in Europe were rejected or restricted between January and April — more than in all of 2025, according to the European Data Center Monitor. It found that pushback had snowballed from local town halls to courts, regulators and parliaments.
Scotland has paused planning approvals for new hyperscale data centers after campaigners called on the government to avoid the "cautionary tale" of Ireland, where overwhelming power demand led to a moratorium.
Constraints have been rising in the Nordics, where investors were drawn to large tracts of land and renewable energy. After a surge in power applications , Denmark passed an emergency law that could see data centers at the back of the queue for grid power applications.
Spain also proposed new data center rules this summer, requiring data centers to source 80% of their electricity from renewables. Projects in the U.K. have stalled after pushback from locals.
Much of the concern centers around water usage , power consumption , electricity prices, and the sheer amount of space that some centers require. There is also little agreement on how many permanent jobs the sector creates, and no precedent for projecting a center's economic value per megawatt.
"The gains of AI are very diffused," Darmouni told CNBC.
"There's definitely been more understanding of the scale of the potential AI build-out and its geographical spread, and perhaps ... more information about how much bigger these are, and that they're a little bit more like giant ghost warehouses that consume a lot of resources and can hurt local communities in some ways."
Europe's denser population, and the fact that many data center operators are U.S. companies, might mean that the backlash hits harder, the professor added.
South Korea, home to tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, sits at the heart of the AI supply chain. In June, its government named AI data centers as one of three major investment projects, alongside semiconductors and physical AI.
But its push to build the infrastructure needed is running into resistance at the local level.
In the Geumcheon district of southwestern Seoul, residents have called for authorities to revoke the building permit and halt construction of a data center near their homes, according to the local government.
In July, officials announced plans to require consent from a majority of residents living within 200 meters of proposed data center sites and to introduce a three-stage system for reviewing projects and mediating disputes.
Residents have also gathered outside the local government office on weekday mornings for months to protest against the project. The demonstrations had continued for 172 days as of mid-August, according to local media .
In Gwacheon, a city just south of Seoul, a local council member proposed an ordinance aimed at protecting nearby residents from risks associated with data centers operating around the clock, including potential fires involving backup batteries.
Despite the pusback, the AI boom shows little sign of slowing down.
But a community's ability "to derail a $10 billion [data center] plan is quite powerful," said Asya Walters, managing director at Alvarez & Marsal.
She told CNBC the business-friendly environment in the U.S. has historically made it easier to overcome pushback.
But in Europe and Asia, there's some "hot and coldness" at the country level about where demand is going, Walters said. The "push and pull" between favorable conditions for data centers and more restrictive regulation can be challenging for investment.
Public backlash can also end up raising costs for operators, because even if they pull out of a project before construction starts, money will likely have already been spent.
Though most capex expenditure happens after the permits are in place, operators spend a lot to reach that point, "so there is some loss that could happen there if they never get the permits," Walters said.
"Digital infrastructure is becoming more visible and it's understandable that communities want to understand what's being built near them, why it's needed and how local impacts are being managed," said Eulalia Flo, vice president of growth and emerging markets, EMEA at Equinix , one of the biggest data center operators in Europe.
"We don't see this as a structural constraint on growth, but the policy environment is genuinely tightening in some markets," said Flo.
But the AI buildout has meant "a misunderstanding of the industry in a very broad sense," according to Dominic Ward, CEO of data center operator Verne.
"We used to be a completely unknown part of the economy," Ward told CNBC. "We were just a black box. We were just a building that had stuff that went in that nobody understood. Now we are one of the fundamental layers driving the economy."
He added: "Now everybody knows where they are, so there's kind of no hiding behind this."

articles.title_orig: Trump promises 'nearly $100' to 20M seniors in latest cash giveaway
articles.title_zh: Trump promises 'nearly $100' to 20M seniors in latest cash giveaway
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump announced late on Friday, Oct. 2, that he will send "nearly $100" to 20 million seniors across the country in his latest effort to promise Americans cash .
To be exact, it's $90 to each of the seniors.
"My Administration will, immediately, begin sending 'Checks' of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums," the president said in the late-night announcement on his social media website Truth Social. "This money will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, a pointless 'Slush Fund' that has only been used by Dumocrats in Congress to pay for the Waste, Fraud, and Abuse."
It’s unclear whether the White House has the authority to divert the cash as Trump says. USA TODAY has reached out to the administration for information.
The promised checks are the president’s latest move to offer Americans money ahead of the upcoming midterms. Trump is not on the ballot but Republicans are expected to face a tough fight from Democrats amid angst over the negative impact Trump’s war on Iran has had on household finances.
Trump, in his announcement Friday, repeated another one of his cash promises tied to the midterms: $5,000 to every U.S. adult "if, and when, the Republicans win."
Critics say the $5,000 amounts to nothing more than a bribe .
According to a USA TODAY review of promises Trump has made about giving Americans cash, the president has a mixed record.
Around 1.45 million U.S. servicemembers received his $1,776 "warrior dividend" checks. However, Americans did not receive supposed $2,000 tariff dividend checks nor checks resulting from Department of Government Efficiency savings. The DOGE savings checks were estimated to be as high as $5,000.
The $100 check announcement comes days after White House officials said they would begin $500 checks to nearly $1 million Americans his administration says were overcharged through the Affordable Care Act's federal exchange for buying health insurance.

articles.title_orig: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.title_zh: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.content_orig:
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.
It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.
Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports , there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".
Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."
"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said.
"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."
Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.
Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".
Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.
The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.
The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday .
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.
The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.
Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title_orig: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.title_zh: Former vendor’s viral post sparks backlash against Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks
articles.content_orig:
Nick Neville , Community Correspondent , Orlando, FL
KISSIMMEE, Fla. – A now former vendor at Kissimmee’s World Food Trucks says she was forced out of the space she rented for about a decade, triggering a viral backlash and calls online for a boycott of the food truck park.
Gabriella Santos, who operated Los Cipotes, posted a video saying she was given just hours to move her food truck after ten years at the location. The post drew millions of views and sparked a heated debate on social media.
Santos told News 6 that her frustration built for years, citing what she describes as safety concerns, rising operating costs, and feeling unsupported.
She also said vendors paid out of pocket for events, absorbed new fees, and saw sales decline as more trucks were added to the park.
“Somebody’s making that extra money, and it’s not us,” Santos said in a Friday interview.
Santos said a lease renewal meeting this week became a boiling point. She claims a manager asked for access to her point-of-sale system, which she believes was framed as a way to determine rent.
“She said wanted access to the POS, and I said ‘Why do you need access to that?’” Santos said. “’Oh it’s because that’s how we’re going to balance how much your rent is going to be.’”
Santos also raised concerns about what she says were new lease terms, including language she interpreted as requiring 60 percent if a renewed lease was later broken.
World Food Trucks publicly disputed that claim, saying in a social media response: “That claim is completely false.”
Santos later clarified during the interview that she was describing her perception of what the changes would mean for her business, not alleging a literal demand for 60 percent of sales.
“I never said that,” she said. “What I said was that they wanted 60 percent of my business because that’s how I feel. That’s my personal feeling of what you’re doing to me. You’re taking my profits.”
She told News 6 she understand the terms to mean the food truck park would have wanted 60 percent of the remainder of the lease agreement.
Santos said after refusing to sign the new lease, she was told to leave by midnight on Thursday. Photos obtained by News 6 show her former spot is now surrounded by tables.
In a statement to News 6, World Food Trucks said in part, “We respect every vendor’s right to share their experience. We also believe disagreements deserve respectful conversation and accurate information. Our vendors pay a fixed weekly rent, rather than a percentage of their food sales, and we remain committed to clear communication with our vendor community.
Our focus is on supporting the more than 100 businesses that make World Food Trucks possible. We invite everyone to visit, meet the people behind the food, and support the local entrepreneurs who have helped build this community.”
Santos said she believes the viral reaction resonated because people see small business owners as vulnerable.
She said she is speaking for other vendors who are too afraid to go public.
“I think people don’t want little people to get bullied,” she said.

articles.title_orig: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.title_zh: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia . Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination” .
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates , where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

This week, Hillsborough County in Florida, which includes Tampa, declared a state of emergency linked to a growing number of dengue cases. So far this year, around 485 cases have been reported in the state , according to the CDC. The disease, which is transmitted by mosquitoes, can cause serious flu-like illness, and one person in Florida has died in the outbreak so far this year, the state’s department of health told media outlets in September.
Seasonal outbreaks of the disease, which affects up to 400 million people worldwide annually , are not unusual in Florida, and they’re often linked to travelers. But this time is a little different, says Michael Johansson, an epidemiologist at Northeastern University. “This is the most locally acquired cases that we've seen in the state,” he says.
Dengue, sometimes called dengue fever, is caused by a collection of viruses carried by mosquitoes , primarily Aedes aegypti . Dengue is endemic in a wide swath of the tropics, and usually, most Americans who have the infection acquire it outside of the U.S. during travel. Dengue symptoms can occur 5-7 days after being bitten and range from mild to severe. They may include painful body aches as well as fever and can last up to 10 days .
However, in parts of the U.S. where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes live, they can bite infected people and start to spread the disease locally. “The general pattern that we see—and we've seen this for more than a decade now—is that there are frequent travel-associated cases” in Florida, says Johansson. “We know we have the right vectors there, especially in southern Florida, where there's lots of Aedes aegypti, and there is some local transmission that occurs. Usually that looks like just one or two cases, but sometimes there are small outbreaks.”
In 2009, when two locally acquired infections were identified in Key West, public-health surveillance revealed that a substantial share of people in the town had markers in their blood showing a recent encounter with dengue , even if they hadn’t had symptoms. That suggests that in an outbreak, dengue is likely to be infecting more people than might immediately be clear from case counts.
One distinctive feature of dengue, however, is that the second time someone is infected is likely to be much worse than the first. Sometimes a second infection can progress to dengue hemorrhagic fever , which can involve bleeding and a drop in blood pressure, and is sometimes fatal.
This pattern, where the second exposure is more dangerous than the first, has complicated attempts to vaccinate people against the disease. In 2017, Sanofi Pasteur, the manufacturer of the dengue vaccine Dengvaxia, alerted the government of the Philippines that serious dengue infections might occur in people who had received the vaccine as their first exposure to the disease. No dengue vaccine is currently available in the U.S.; Dengvaxia was available starting in 2019 but in 2025 was discontinued by the manufacturer, which cited low demand.
So far, dengue has not established a permanent foothold in the continental U.S., says Johansson. There are a few reasons why that might be: large numbers of people in Florida, where Aedes aegypti thrive, stay within air-conditioned spaces when they’re most active, which means chains of transmission tend to be short.
And the mosquitoes themselves are not particularly adventurous. They tend to stay close to home, within about a 100-meter range, so “it takes people to move the virus around,” says Johansson. If someone who’s infected doesn’t travel, the virus doesn’t either.
There is no cure for dengue; the only treatments are for symptoms. If you are in an area with mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the best way to protect yourself is to avoid mosquito bites. Keep windows closed or use screens, cover as much of your skin as possible with clothing when outdoors, and use mosquito repellent, says Johansson.
Keep yards free of containers that could fill with water and serve as breeding zones for mosquitoes. You’ll have to be vigilant: “These mosquitoes in particular, they can breed in a plastic bag that's collected a little bit of rainwater,” says Johansson.
Cooler weather brings relief. “We're getting to the time of year when things are cooling down, so we should expect a decrease in transmission,” says Johansson. “However, it's still hot in Florida right now”—so it’s not time to drop your guard yet.

On Thursday, October 1st, representatives of the Ukrainian Catholic Archeparchy of Philadelphia attended “An Evening with Evan Gershkovich” hosted by the World Affairs Council of Philadelphia (WAC).
In March 2023 shortly after the one-year anniversary of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Evan Gershkovich, an American reporter for the Wall Street Journal , was arrested and charged with espionage by FSB agents in Russia. After a sham trial, he was sentenced to 16 years in a Russian prison only to be released after 16 months as part of a prisoner exchange.
During a fireside chat, WAC President & CEO Lauren Swartz engaged Gershkovich in conversation about his newly released book This Cursed Beautiful Land , a memoir of his unlawful imprisonment. Gershkovich spoke about how he admittedly misread all the signals and was lured into a trap at the time of his arrest. He discussed at length how he understood from the beginning that he was part of Russia’s plan to ‘beef-up its negotiating leverage’. He understood that he would be treated with a certain privilege. Almost immediately Gershkovich realized that he wouldn’t be tortured or interrogated in the same manner as other journalists, siting the barbaric and inhumane torture of Victoria Roshchyna, a Ukrainian journalist who was arrested around the same time as Gershkovich.
The Ukrainian Catholic Archeparchy is a non-profit member of the World Affairs Council of Philadelphia and was a promotional partner for this event.

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), a house and a Volkswagen, plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been higher still if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.
after newsletter promotion
The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

Home › News and Business › Business and Law
As the U.S. Senate adjourns until after the November midterm elections, a familiar concern for backers of the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act has surfaced: Will time run out?
The next step for the legislation, as we’ve covered, is for it to move through the Senate. There was palpable momentum after the bill cleared the house in September . And previously, Sens. Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) secured filibuster-proof majority with 61 senators supporting it.
Most observers believe it will pass in the Senate, and President Donald Trump has expressed his support for the legislation previously. The president would then need to simply sign the bill for the mandate to take effect.
But the bill has to reach the Senate floor for a vote first, and there’s a scant few days left in this current congressional cycle. The 2023 version failed to pass in the Senate after efforts that December fell short .
The AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act’s advocates eyed getting the Senate version of the bill on the floor before the senior chamber cleared for its midterm election recess. That did not happen, and the Senate will not return to the Capitol until the week of Nov. 9, according to The Hill .
If the clock runs out at the end of the year, the process completely resets . Any legislation that fails to pass before the current Congress officially ends on Jan. 3 dies, forcing supporters to reintroduce the bill from scratch next year.
And when the Senate returns from hiatus, it will face a logjam of legislative priorities.
As The Hill noted, the return begins a lame-duck session. When asked about pushing so much work into November and December, Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) sarcastically called the upcoming scramble their “golden era.”
The Senate has only eight working days scheduled for November and 14 for December, including Fridays, which are rarely used for floor action.
But the National Association of Broadcasters continues to express optimism. “We’re on the one-yard line, and the momentum behind the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act remains incredibly strong,” NAB Vice President of Communications Carrie Healey told Inside Radio .
As we’ve reported, the bill requires the DOT to issue a rule within one year requiring AM radio capabilities to be standard in all new passenger vehicles sold in the United States.
The U.S. Congressional Budget Office reported the bill would impact roughly 2 to 2.5 million vehicles every year for models currently manufactured or planned without built-in AM receiving capability, according to its March cost estimate.
CBO estimates that implementing the bill will cost the federal government a total of $1 million over a five-year period.

articles.title_orig: D.A. in Cornell Rape Inquiry Declined to Review Additional Evidence
articles.title_zh: D.A. in Cornell Rape Inquiry Declined to Review Additional Evidence
articles.content_orig:
Outrage is building as the case involving a Cornell University student allegedly gang raped in a fraternity house in 2024 continues to garner national attention, with the state’s governor vowing she “will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug.”
Snapchat messages , a Cornell disciplinary panel’s decision and a cache of documents from the university’s formal Title IX investigation obtained by The New York Times have shed new light on what may have happened in the fraternity house, Doe’s reported frame of mind at certain points throughout that night and how her understanding of the events changed as she processed her trauma in the weeks that followed.
Cornell is facing scrutiny because the university initially said campus police investigated the allegations in 2024 and “shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office.” But the school later changed its statement , now saying police investigated the allegations in 2024 and “shared the victim’s sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot” with the DA’s office.
The DA previously said his office did not bring criminal charges because of Doe’s six-page statement. He later said his office had access to some Snapchat messages exchanged during the alleged assault in a group chat titled, “Chi Phi Actives.” Images of one Snapchat chain obtained by CNN include a photo of Doe in a room at the fraternity house during the time she describes being assaulted.
‘I am Jane Doe’: Online campaign to protect Cornell plaintiff
Doe made an explicit allegation of rape in her interview that was not included in the six-page statement furnished to prosecutors, according to WCBS.
Although Doe did recount being hit and feeling emotionally coerced in the statement, it did not include some stronger language or allegations she used in her interview, according to The New York Times, citing documents it obtained.
Among the documents also obtained by the Times , were records showing the district attorney’s office declined to review any additional evidence gathered by the campus police department beyond the six-page statement signed by Doe.
A Cornell police investigator spoke to a member of the district attorney’s staff on November 25, 2024, about reviewing additional evidence, the Times said. By that time, university police had conducted more interviews and reviewed chat messages, the Times report said.
But prosecutors did not express interest in the additional evidence because they had decided that, based on Doe’s statement, “Criminal charges would not be pursued in this case,” a Cornell police investigator said in a note documenting the call.
When reached for comment, the district attorney staff member referred all questions to the district attorney, the Times reported.
Van Houten, the district attorney, told the Times by email that any additional records gathered by the Cornell police were “not pertinent to our analysis because we had Jane Doe’s comprehensive account of the events.”
CNN reached out to Van Houten’s office for comment Friday.
CNN obtained a copy of a heavily redacted, 99-page document summarizing key evidence included in a Cornell disciplinary panel’s decision, which supports the Times’ findings about how Doe later came to understand the night’s events as assault. The panel’s decision details more than 50 interviews, including with six of the seven accused men.
The initial university investigation led to suspensions and expulsions for the accused students, according to Doe’s attorney, the barring of the fraternity chapter from campus and the launch of a sexual assault task force. Four of the Chi Phi fraternity members acknowledged having sexual contact with Doe but said their interactions had been consensual. The others denied participating in sexual encounters, the Times reported.
Amid the renewed investigation, court documents show a Chi Phi fraternity member named as a defendant in Doe’s civil suit has been petitioning New York state courts to invalidate a university disciplinary decision that found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation.
Cornell student groups are planning a protest on campus Monday to “hold our university responsible,” according to an Instagram post from Students for a Democratic Cornell and several other campus organizations.

articles.title_orig: From Rifle to the world: DM Vans surpasses 800-van mark
articles.title_zh: From Rifle to the world: DM Vans surpasses 800-van mark
articles.content_orig:
psullivan@postindependent.com
DM Vans builds its camper vans today in a state-of-the-art, 20,000-square-foot facility in Rifle.
The company has come a long way from the original production site: the Vail Mountain School parking lot.
DM Vans co-founder Matt Fesler built this first van out of necessity.
“I wanted something I could travel through the mountains with, bring my skis, bring my bikes, bring my golf clubs, and stay in comfortably,” Fesler said. “At the time, there really wasn’t something out there on the market that fit what I was looking for within my budget.”
Felser was a teacher at Vail Mountain School at the time and needed a vehicle that could serve as a portable base camp for his adventures.
With the help of YouTube tutorials and some friends, the first Dave and Matt, or DM, van came to fruition in the Vail Mountain School parking lot.
Fesler and his friend, and eventual DM Vans co-founder, Dave Ramsay, soon realized that they had done more than build the vehicle that Fesler was looking for.
The pair “realized that (they) had something, something that was simple, reliable, easier to use than what was on the market, and obviously more affordable,” Fesler said.
After living in that first van for nine months, which he “loved to death,” Fesler got the itch to build more.
“So I sold that first one, used that to build two, sold two, built four, sold four, built eight, and yeah, here we are, eight years later, and 800 vans,” Fesler said.
The 800 Ram ProMaster vans which DM vans transformed into parking-spot-sized homes are now spread across 48 states, and the company shows no signs of slowing down.
Although the 30-person team, and sheer scale of the operation are a far cry from the early days of DM Vans, some things have stayed the same.
“We’ve used the tagline ‘everything you need, nothing you don’t’ from day one,” Fesler said. “That was kind of how I wanted to approach it in terms of something that was simple and reliable that would get me from A to B comfortably and allow me to stay there and pursue my passions, and it is amazing how that design philosophy has stayed from day one through now.”
That does not mean DM Vans has shied away from technological advances to improve their product, however.
With smaller, lighter and more powerful lithium batteries on the market, DM Vans can run heating, air conditioning, running water, refrigeration and other appliances off relatively small power supply.
Using a computer numerical control, or CNC, machine, the company can cut out wooden parts with precision and ease.
DM Vans hopes to build 145 vans in the coming year.
The combination of the “van-life” boom and navigating the coronavirus pandemic gave the pair their fair share of obstacles to navigate.

“Dave (Ramsay) and I joke a lot that we very much had the best MBA program you could possibly go on in our eight-year journey here of the highest of highs, lowest of lows, but are really excited for the stability that we now have as a business, the incredible employees we have in Rifle and around Colorado,” Fesler said.
After eight years of successful business and growth, Fesler is proud of how far the company has come.
“The numbers of businesses that go out of business after five years are staggering, right? To make it to 10 is truly something that would be that peak moment for us, and so just being here doing something that we love is the thing that makes me the most proud,” Fesler said.

Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
UPDATE: Apple has confirmed a problem affecting the AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max.
"We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls," Apple tells PCMag. "We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today. These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.”
The update is intended to prevent this from happening to other phones, so if your iPhone has already lost service, you'll need to take it in for replacement. The carrier setting update is expected in the next two weeks, but you can force it via Settings > General > About .
At this point, it's only affecting the iPhone 18 Pro Max on AT&T.
Original Story: Ever since the iPhone 18 Pro Max launched last month, AT&T customers have complained about being unable to make calls, send texts, or use cellular data. According to MacRumors , the carrier acknowledged the issue in a text message to customers this week and recommended an immediate software upgrade to fix the issue.
“Hi, it’s AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately,” reads AT&T’s message to customers.
Apple's iOS 27.0.1 began rolling out to iPhone users on Monday. The release notes mention patches for a Face ID bug and camera-zooming issues on iPhone 18 Pro models, as well as a fix for an unresponsive screen issue . No mention of AT&T issues, though.
Even after updating to iOS 27.0.1, cellular issues persist for some AT&T customers. "I cannot make or receive cellular phone calls on the brand-new phone I set up this morning," Lindsay Robertson, a writer and editor from Brooklyn, tells PCMag. "Nor can I make or receive them on my old phone. AT&T, you have ONE JOB!"
Robertson now plans to visit the AT&T store this weekend to re-activate her old phone before going to the Apple Store to get a replacement iPhone 18 Pro Max. "I will just have to pray that all that work fixed it," she says. "I spent over two hours talking to AT&T support this morning, with each minute becoming more infuriating."
It's unclear whether the issue lies with the carrier or the iPhone hardware. Neither Apple nor AT&T has explained the cause. If you want to try your luck, you can update your iPhone software by going to Settings > General > Software Update.
An AT&T spokesperson tells us that the Apple update should "address an issue that may affect calls, data, texts, and 911 calls on a small number of Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max phones," adding, "Our top priority is ensuring customers can stay connected when they need it most, and we are working with Apple to make it right.”
On Apple’s Community forum , we spotted a few customers saying they visited an Apple Store, where staff ordered replacement units for them. articles.title_orig: Lemon Hill hosted the world for Fan Fest. Now, Philadelphia will spend millions to improve it for locals.
articles.title_zh: Lemon Hill hosted the world for Fan Fest. Now, Philadelphia will spend millions to improve it for locals.
articles.content_orig:
The FIFA Fan Festival brought hundreds of thousands of people from across the planet to Philadelphia's Lemon Hill for a celebration of soccer this summer. Now, as the massive stage and vendor tents have left the natural scenery, the park will undergo a different transformation.
"In spite of the fact that Fan Fest did take away the park for a while, I think it became sort of the momentum generator for what's to come," Aparna Palantino, who heads the city's Capital Program Office, said.
CBS News Philadelphia was the only TV station to get a first look at the nearly $7 million in upgrades and enhancements planned for the rolling hills in East Fairmount Park.
At the center of the project is a new 43,500-square-foot age-inclusive playground to replace the current structure, which has been in place for decades.
Palantino said the playground will incorporate the park's natural features, like slides that use Lemon Hill's natural hillside.
"We wanted it to fit within the context of the park. It is a lovely, very natural, pristine setting. Has a lot of historical character. And it was important for us to maintain that," Palantino said.
Aside from the playground, the plan includes renovations to the popular basketball courts at Lemon Hill and to the nearby baseball field. Two new ADA-accessible picnic pavilions with seating will be built. More than 50 light posts are set to be added around the park, increasing lighting and safety. And crews plan to plant more than 100 new trees.
"Across the site, we want to return a lot of the tree canopy that was lost over the years," Palantino said.
Officials said the city has looked into making many of these changes for years but never had the funding to do it. That changed with the FIFA Fan Festival, when officials built partnerships that got the project across the finish line.
Officials said Philadelphia Soccer 2026 and the William Penn Foundation will kick in a total of $4 million for the plans, with the city picking up the rest of the bill.
Some enhancements were also made prior to Fan Fest opening in June. New walking paths were added for better access to the park. Roads were paved. Trees were trimmed, and invasive plants were cleared out.
But for this portion, Palantino said they focused on what community members told them they wanted here.
"We had over 200 individual community members participate in over 300 surveys to get their feedback on what they wanted to see," Palantino said. "We have very good stewards and neighbors who take care of this park on a regular basis. And it was really important that all of their voices were heard."
Signs are already posted showing some of the planned changes. The current playground and basketball courts are fenced off, getting ready for the changes. City officials on Monday will host a ceremonial planting of the first new tree.
Officials hope the work can be done and upgrades open to the public in the spring.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | FlyDubai Attacker Had Been Banned From Flying by Oman for Radical Views
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | FlyDubai Attacker Had Been Banned From Flying by Oman for Radical Views
articles.content_orig:
Attorney general says ‘terrorist attack’ was attempted by suspect who is said to have been barred from flying by Oman because of extremist views
The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used a crash axe to attempt to carry out a “terrorist attack” during the flight, the United ⁠Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to a state news agency.
The UAE statement cited the prosecutor general as saying the co-pilot also tried to take control of the plane during Wednesday’s attack on the Israel-bound flight. Passengers and crew intervened to subdue the co-pilot and stabilise the plane. Officials said the co-pilot’s actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board by sending it into a sharp plunge.
A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for ⁠use during emergencies.
The co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a person familiar with the matter said. He was then hired by the United Arab Emirates-based airline flydubai, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. Oman’s barring of him was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
The co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian, according to a regional official with knowledge of the investigation.
How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators . Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots out of its airspace who come from nations with which it does not maintain diplomatic relations. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.
The official confirmed that the co-pilot worked with Oman’s national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views. He was later moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, the official said.
Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other western governments, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.
UAE senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash on Friday called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act”. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation” but provided no evidence.
The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed loud noises to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the plane. It made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Both the captain and co-pilot were taken to the UAE as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.

articles.title_orig: Apple changes full-disk access permissions to curb abuse from AI agents
articles.title_zh: Apple changes full-disk access permissions to curb abuse from AI agents
articles.content_orig:
Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories.
Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully.
Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse.
“The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in,” Singleton said. “Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”
Singleton’s implication was clear. Muse could have read Aten’s Messages communications only if he had enabled both settings, and if so, the columnist had only himself—and certainly not Meta—to blame.
Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert Patrick Wardle, who questioned Singleton’s denial. His reasoning: “From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.” I asked Meta how Muse couldn’t read messages when the app had full disk access, while every other app with that privilege could. Meta PR’s only response was to requote Singleton saying: “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac App is opt-in. Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”
Now, Apple is setting the record straight. In explaining why it was going to make changes to the FDA permission setting, the company wrote:
Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.
As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.
Apple didn’t name Meta, Muse, or any other app or developer by name. Even though there are no known reports of other apps abusing FDA to read messages and browsing history, it’s certainly possible Friday’s statement wasn’t referring to the Muse incident. Then again, the timing of the announcement—coming on the heels of a major social media uproar—makes the possibility likely. And at a minimum, Apple’s statements seem to contradict Singleton’s denial that it’s not possible for Muse to read Messages content without the connector enabled. Meta PR didn’t respond to questions sent Friday.
Apple’s announcement came 11 days after Wardle disclosed a Muse configuration that allowed any app or code running on a Mac—including commands injected through the increasingly effective ClickFix attacks—to take full control of the AI assistant . From there, the attacker could access the same resources Muse could. It also comes after Amazon blocked Muse from its platform because, Amazon said, all such apps “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.”
Taken together, the events suggest that Muse may not be worthy of the extraordinary access it must have to work as billed by Meta. People who use the assistant should configure permissions carefully, though as Aten’s experience suggests, that precaution only goes so far.

articles.title_orig: Unemployment Rate Ticks Higher as Job Growth Slows
articles.title_zh: Unemployment Rate Ticks Higher as Job Growth Slows
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
U.S. employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, and the unemployment rate rose a tenth of a percentage point to 4.2%, the Labor Department announced Friday. Both results failed to meet expectations, as analysts had projected job growth of about 90,000 and a steady unemployment rate for the month.
Job growth in the previous two months was moved lower, as well, with the numbers for July reduced by 31,000, moving the final tally to a loss of 10,000, and August falling by 29,000 to 133,0000.
The healthcare sector provided the majority of the growth in September, as it has for many months, adding a weaker-than-usual 17,000 jobs. Construction firms created 11,000 jobs, and manufacturers 9,000.
Employment in federal, state and local governments fell by 17,000, while professional and business services firms cut 9,000 jobs.
Wages grew 3.0% on an annual basis, the smallest 12-month gain since May 2021.
What the analysts are saying: Analysts downplayed the miss in the top-line numbers, saying the labor market appears to be holding more or less steady, despite the monthly variations. From July through September, job growth has averaged 51,000 per month, a level many economists see as a stable level in a "low hire, low fire" job market.
"The September employment report came in a little bit softer than expected but overall wasn't too worrying," JPMorgan's Michael Feroli wrote in a note to clients. Feroli pointed out that the unemployment rate rose because 485,000 people entered the workforce, a positive sign about the strength of the economy. And he described the three-month growth average as being "close to most estimates of trend monthly growth in the labor supply, i.e. breakeven job growth."
RSM Chief Economist Joseph Brusuelas said the labor market appears to have settled into a new normal, shaped by political policy and basic demographics. "Growth in the domestic supply of labor will remain soft given the well-known long-term demographic challenges posed by the retirement of baby boomers and restrictive immigration policies," he said in a research note . "Soft readings like September's and an underlying trend of around 50,000 new jobs added monthly will be the norm over the next two years at the least."
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, emphasized the same point. "The September jobs report tells us the 'low hire, low fire' job market is still here," she said on X. "There was hope that hiring was picking up, but it's stabilizing at a low ~50k a month." Long noted that job growth is being driven largely by two sectors: healthcare and the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Long added the latest data confirms the worry that millions of American workers are feeling "financial pain," with the lowest year-over-year wage growth in five years (see her chart below). "Inflation has eaten up all wage gains for the average worker since April," she wrote . "Many people are having to make hard choices about what to buy and what to skimp on right now. Yes, consumption is still strong (mainly due to wealthier Americans and people dipping into savings or credit cards), but a lot of people have to think hard about every dollar they spend."
Fed may sit tight: The soft jobs and wage data indicate that the labor market is not contributing to inflation, reducing pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting at the end of the month.
According to CME's FedWatch tool , traders now assign a 22% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the meeting, a big drop from the 35% reading a week ago.
"This report strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to remain patient," said Adam Schickling, a senior economist at Vanguard, per CNBC. "The labor market has not deteriorated sharply, but there is also little evidence that it has meaningfully strengthened, giving policymakers reason to wait for additional data."
