articles.title_orig: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
articles.title_zh: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
articles.content_orig:
Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election
S hortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.
“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.
Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.
On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.
Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.
Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro , 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.
“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum , is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.
“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.
Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs ” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land .
While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.
Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth , but it is currently at a low point , with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.
“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”
A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.
At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.
Privileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals was one of the conditions Washington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has offered those natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.
“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup to overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.
“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.
As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.
Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he took fourth place in Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – some shelved , others still under investigation – has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.
Unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen , and average incomes have risen, but so has household debt – something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated and Lula banned days before the vote.
The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving supreme court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.
Many therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from a simple transfer of his father’s voter base and from an anti-Lula vote .
“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.
Actor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed by Jair Bolsonaro’s election that she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.
She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.
She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.
“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.

articles.content_orig:
Dominic Rosales, a 16-year-old goaltender from Hollister, has been selected to represent Team USA's junior inline hockey team at the 2026 World Skate Games in Asunción, Paraguay, marking the biggest tournament of his career.
"I just want to, like, take the most out of it, experience how South America is going to be, having to represent Team USA. Play with my friends, you know, I think that will be the most I want to take out of it. Obviously, winning a gold medal would be cool too," Rosales said.
A gold medal would be a fitting achievement for Rosales, who has already proven himself as one of the nation's elite young goaltenders.
Rosales grew up watching his father, Diego, play as a goalie, inspiring him to pursue the position himself. His passion for the sport started early, even leading him to dress up as a goalie for Halloween.
"Me and my buddy just MacGyvered that thing. We just got a bunch of tape, cardboard, and hard foam, and we made his own little set. He was super happy. After Halloween, he used it every single day outside. He was able to slide across in the living room, and he thought he was the next goalie, you know? And it worked," Diego said.
Diego has been instrumental in supporting his son's dream, working three jobs over the years to ensure Dominic could pursue his passion for hockey.
"I think the most rewarding things out of this, sure, I'll take another job, another shift, do extra jobs here and there. I think the fact that he loves the sport makes it so much worth it, right? And we can look past all the rest of it," Diego said.
As Rosales prepares to compete on the world stage, he carries the pride of his hometown with him.
"It fills me with pride because I know Hollister will have my back and support me. They've been supporting me with this journey. I think, definitely coming back, I'll have a lot of pride. I'm happy I'm able to represent Hollister, a small town," Rosales said.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike unconscious and on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike unconscious and on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike, the woman who survived an execution attempt in Tennessee earlier this week, remains hospitalized in critical condition, her lawyers said in a new statement Friday.
She is unconscious, intubated and breathing through a ventilator. The death row inmate is also being treated for “significant injuries to both arms” sustained when two lethal injections of pentobarbital failed to kill her.
At one point, Pike said it felt like her arm was exploding, and she could be heard whimpering, according to her legal team.
“We are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” attorney Luke Ihnen said in a statement. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”
The state of Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death Wednesday night by lethal injection for a murder she committed when she was 18.
Pike, now 50, has been on death row for decades and would have been the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.
NBC News earlier reported that there was no emergency medical oxygen in the execution room in case something went wrong. Medical professionals had to retrieve it from elsewhere.
Pike’s attorneys detailed her condition in a new emergency motion filed Friday asking the state to preserve all evidence from the failed execution attempt.
“In the words of one media witness: we have a lot of questions and the Department of Correction has a lot of answers that it needs to provide to the public about what happened here. We agree,” the motion reads.
In their filing, the lawyers described a painful and chaotic scene that unfolded in front of several witnesses, and that they said could have been prevented with the proper care and training.
Medical staff failed to follow basic protocol, like ensuring the needles used were fresh, functional and inserted properly, according to the motion. Further, the state did not heed Pike’s concerns prior to the procedure that preexisting medical conditions could make lethal injection difficult to complete, the motion says.
The motion accuses the department of corrections of “inflicting a cruel and unusual punishment on Ms. Pike through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol.”
The Tennessee Attorney General did not immediately return a request for comment on the new filing. A spokesperson for the state department of corrections said the agency does not comment on pending litigation.
At a news conference Thursday, Stephen Ferrell and another of Pike’s attorneys, Randall Spivey, detailed how the execution attempt went wrong . Spivey, who was in the room, recalled Pike saying she was in pain, and like she felt like her arm was about to “explode.”
“It’s not supposed to be a cruel and an unusual execution,” criminologist Deborah Denno told NBC News. “The goal is to kill somebody, but to kill them within means or in a reasonable way, where there’s not going to be pain and suffering.”
According to Friday’s filing, the execution process lasted longer than two hours. Pike’s legal team filed emergency motions to halt the execution in multiple courts before the prison called an ambulance.
“Even then,” it continues, “attorneys for the State of Tennessee argued that TDOC had no obligation to render life-saving care to Ms. Pike.”
NBC News contributor Dr. Natalie Azar, a rheumatologist, said the pain Pike described could be attributed to pentobarbital flowing into her arm instead of straight into her veins. That would be painful with any medication, Azar said, but the specific properties of pentobarbital would make the experience exceptionally uncomfortable.
The scenario would also result in Pike being administered a less-than-lethal dose. It was enough to suppress her respiratory system but not enough to kill her, Azar explained. The question of how long Pike’s brain was deprived on oxygen will be central to her prognosis.
“There is no reversal of pentobarbital. There is no medicine or antidote,” she said. “You have to basically wait for the liver to metabolize the drug and get it out of your system.”
Pike was convicted in the 1995 murder case. She and two other teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, Knoxville police said at the time. Pike was sentenced to death. A number of last-minute legal efforts to stop Pike’s execution were unsuccessful.
Jesse Kirsch is a correspondent based in Miami reporting across all NBC News platforms.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_zh: Shivon Zilis says she was 'let go' from relationship with Elon Musk
articles.content_orig:
The mother of four of Elon Musk’s children has claimed that their relationship ended “with no warning”.
Shivon Zilis, 40, said: “It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes.”
Mr Musk, 55, fathered four children with Ms Zilis over the past five years, all conceived via in-vitro fertilisation (IVF).
Ms Zilis, who is the director of operations and special projects at one of Musk’s companies Neuralink, posted on X on Friday: “I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness.
“I loved being that counterbalancing place of safety, sense of calm, and love – and delighted in bringing a smile back to his face when he was down. I will miss him dearly.”
Ms Zilis was responding to an X post, which showed Mr Musk had unfollowed her on the platform.
She also posted a screenshot of a text exchange with a contact listed as “E”, which appears to be Mr Musk.
In the messages, Mr Musk said last week that he loved her and that he would have invited her to the state dinner between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping last week, where he was a guest.
“I didn’t realise that this Xi dinner included significant other [sic],” he wrote.
Details of the relationship between Mr Musk and Ms Zilis emerged during a high-profile lawsuit against his competitor OpenAI, where Ms Zilis previously served on the board.
Mr Musk was an early investor in OpenAI , and Ms Zilis often acted as a go-between after the relationship between the billionaire and the company soured.
She testified during the trial in May, revealing that her relationship with Mr Musk began as a “one-off” during a corporate event in 2015.
Mr Musk later offered to be a sperm donor when Ms Zilis decided to have children as a single mother. Their relationship later evolved into a romantic partnership.
Mr Musk reportedly has 14 children with four women.
During his time campaigning for Mr Trump in 2024, some people close to him were apparently worried about his “fixation on having more children,” The New York Times reported last year.
In February 2025, as Mr Musk was overseeing the work of the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge), he appeared in the Oval Office with his son , X Æ A-Xii, on his shoulders.
Mr Musk had reportedly been battling with X Æ A-Xii’s mother, Grimes, who had apparently privately complained that they agreed to keep him out of the public eye.
Mr Musk has not commented on the end of his relationship with Ms Zilis.

articles.title_orig: Guns, voting, immigration and more: The biggest cases the Supreme Court will take up in its new term
articles.title_zh: Guns, voting, immigration and more: The biggest cases the Supreme Court will take up in its new term
articles.content_orig:
The Supreme Court begins its latest term on Monday with a docket full of high-stakes cases that touch on some of the most contentious issues in American politics, including guns, voting and transgender rights.
This will be the second full term for the nation's highest court since President Trump returned to the White House. The previous term, which wrapped up in June, was packed with landmark rulings in a long list of major cases , including Trump's tariffs, birthright citizenship and a slate of key immigration decisions.
The justices will likely take on additional cases over the course of the term, but there are already plenty of pivotal cases for the court to consider in the coming months.
Here's a rundown of the big cases headed to the Supreme Court this term and what their eventual rulings might mean for the country.
Over the past two decades, the Supreme Court has issued a series of decisions that have significantly expanded gun rights. It could go even further next term when it considers whether laws banning certain semiautomatic rifles , like the AR-15, violate the Second Amendment.
This category of guns was banned nationwide for a decade until Congress allowed the law to expire in 2004. Similar bans are currently in place in about a dozen states. Gun rights groups have challenged those laws , arguing that it's unconstitutional for these specific types of firearms to be singled out for bans that don't apply to other guns under the Second Amendment.
A dozen states currently require voters to show proof of citizenship — like a birth certificate or passport — when they register to vote. The Supreme Court will consider the legality of these requirements again, this time in a challenge to Arizona's latest proof-of-citizenship law in the case Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota . The law is currently blocked by a federal circuit court ruling that called some of its provisions "unlawful measures of voter suppression." Republicans have asked the court to overturn that decision and allow the requirements in Arizona and elsewhere to remain in place.
The court's final ruling could have massive implications for voting across the United States. Non-citizen voting is extraordinarily rare and there are already legal measures in place in every state to ensure that only ballots from citizens are counted. That hasn't stopped Republicans from pushing for new laws requiring voters to prove their citizenship. Ballot measures aimed at curbing noncitizen voting will be considered by voters in six states in November. Trump's signature elections bill, the SAVE America Act, would apply the requirements nationwide.
Some researchers argue that, rather than preventing fraud, these laws create hurdles that prevent eligible voters from casting their ballots. According to one estimate, as many as 21 million people across the United States lack the documents they would need to be able to vote under proof-of-citizenship requirements.
One of the many points of debate around transgender rights in recent years has been the extent of parents' authority over decisions involving their trans-identifying children. The court will weigh in on this issue once again this term when it hears a case challenging a Washington law that gives the operators of emergency shelters the option not to contact parents of runaway transgender youth who are seeking gender-affirming care. A group of parents has sued, arguing that the law violates their parental rights "to raise their child in accordance with the child's biological sex."
The pending case runs along similar lines to one decided earlier this year, in which the justices ruled in favor of parents seeking to block a California law that limited when schools can "out" transgender students to their families.
In 2020, Colorado voters approved a ballot measure to establish universal preschool throughout the state. As part of the program, state funding is only available to private preschools that meet certain "equal opportunity" standards — including a willingness to enroll LGBTQ students. Two Catholic preschools sued the state , arguing that they were being discriminated against on the basis of their religion by being denied state funding for standing by their beliefs. The state contends that there is no discrimination present because its rules apply to all schools, whether they're religiously affiliated or not.
In two similar cases over the past decade, the court has come down on the side of the schools, ruling that states generally can't exclude religious schools from public programs simply because they are religious.
After siding with Trump in a series of immigration-related rulings during its most recent term, the court has agreed to take on three more cases that touch on the heart of the president's immigration agenda.
The headline case, which the court agreed to hear just a few days before the start of the term, centers around the Trump administration's mandatory detention policy for undocumented immigrants. Historically, migrants who are being considered for removal have had the opportunity to apply for release from detention while they wait for their case to be decided by the courts. Trump changed that policy, causing tens of thousands of immigrants to remain in detention while they await potential deportation. Lower courts have split on the question of whether it's legal for the administration to uniformly deny detained migrants the right to a bond hearing. Now, the Supreme Court will have the final say.
A second case centers around Trump's migrant detention policies for a different group of immigrants. The central question is whether migrants with a criminal history, including those who were in the country legally, can be held in detention centers indefinitely, or if they have the right to challenge their detention in court. The case involves two lawful permanent residents who were detained for what they argue was an "unreasonably prolonged" period without a bond hearing. Immigration detention has become a major source of debate during Trump's second term, amid reports of unsafe conditions at detention centers and a striking increase in the number of deaths among detainees.
The third immigration case involves immigrants who had once been granted asylum in the United States, had that status revoked and now argue that they should be eligible to become lawful permanent residents. The government argues, and lower courts have agreed so far, that only immigrants with active asylum protection can apply for a green card.
Over the past few years, the Supreme Court has significantly narrowed the government's power to regulate greenhouse emissions in a series of landmark rulings. Next term, it will take up another case that could close off yet another pathway that municipalities have used to try to fight climate change.
Lawmakers in Boulder, Colo., have sued oil and gas companies for their role in perpetuating climate change. Those companies have asked the Supreme Court to block the lawsuit. They contend, and the Trump administration agrees , that only the federal government has the power to seek these types of damages because the impacts of climate change go far beyond Boulder's jurisdiction. Several other cities and some states have filed similar suits against the fossil fuel industry. The court could invalidate all of them if it rules in the companies' favor.
The court will decide whether juries in criminal trials must have 12 jurors . That's already the law in most of the country, but a half-dozen states allow for as few as six jurors in certain cases. The case centers around Hamed Kian, a Florida chiropractor who was convicted of practicing after his license had been suspended following allegations of inappropriate contact with patients. Kian's attorneys argue that the small jury violated his constitutional right to a fair and speedy trial.

articles.title_orig: GOP super PAC cancels spending in North Carolina Senate race, shifting money to Kansas
articles.title_zh: GOP super PAC cancels spending in North Carolina Senate race, shifting money to Kansas
articles.content_orig:
A top Republican super PAC is canceling its ad spending in the Senate race in North Carolina and launching a new ad effort in Kansas, the latest sign the fight for the majority is shifting to red states amid an increasingly tough landscape for the GOP.
The new moves from the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, were first reported by Semafor as a “pause” in spending, confirmed by two people with knowledge of the decision.
After the ad-tracking firm AdImpact reported the group was also removing funds from North Carolina, one person familiar with the decision confirmed that the group is canceling the ads planned for October.
Ad spending decisions can provide clear signals about the races parties and outside groups view as the most competitive and further out of reach.
SLF’s move to direct resources to Kansas underscores how Democrats are putting traditionally Republican states in play as they try to net four seats to take control of the Senate. Democrats will need to win multiple states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024, in addition to defending seats in battleground states.
As Election Day draws closer, Democrats are growing more optimistic about their chances as Trump’s approval ratings drop and voters express frustrations with high costs and the Iran war.
The race in Kansas between GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton has become more competitive in the homestretch, even though the state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
So far, SLF has reserved more than $8 million in airtime in Kansas, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
SLF had been actively involved in North Carolina, where former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley is facing former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat. In September, the group spent more than $17 million on the race, according to AdImpact.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance also each traveled to the state last month to boost Whatley, whom the president personally encouraged to run for the open seat.
But the decision to pause spending in North Carolina, a perennial battleground, is a sign that the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is drifting away from the GOP.
“I am worried about him. I hope he wins,” Trump told reporters Friday of Whatley. “He’s a great man.”
Republicans have been pessimistic for weeks about their prospects in the state, with Cooper leading in recent polling and outspending Whatley.
The party’s level of confidence in their chances of defeating Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia has also been dwindling, but one person familiar with SLF’s spending noted the group has not paused its spending in that race. Trump won Georgia by just 2 points in 2024.
Still, SLF has focused the bulk of its resources on other hotly contested Senate races.
In September, SLF spent $78 million on ads in Texas through an affiliated group, and SLF itself spent nearly $33 million in Ohio. Elsewhere, the group last month spent $16 million in Michigan, $15 million in Iowa, $13 million in Maine, $10 million in Georgia, $8 million in Alaska and $5 million in New Hampshire, according to AdImpact.
In the month of October through the Nov. 3 election, SLF’s Texas group has booked $48 million in ads, while SLF is set to spend $40 million in Ohio, $18 million in Michigan, $17 million in Maine, $16 million in Georgia, nearly $14 million in Iowa, $8 million in New Hampshire and $5 million in Alaska.
Trump carried Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska all by double digits in 2024.
Even as SLF looks to spend its resources elsewhere, the North Carolina Senate candidates are still bracing for a hotly contested race.
Whatley spokesman DJ Griffin said in a statement that Cooper recently noted Democrats are often ahead “until they’re not.”
“Undecided Voters who break late decide the election in North Carolina and the majority of those Late-Breakers typically go Republican,” Griffin said. “We feel confident we have the resources to highlight Career Politician Roy Cooper’s 40 Years of Failures and win in November.”
Cooper campaign manager Jeff Allen also suggested the race is still competitive, noting in a statement that a Democrat has not been elected to the Senate in North Carolina in nearly 20 years and describing North Carolina as “a 50-50 state.”
“We’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them, while Michael Whatley will continue to enrich himself at their expense,” Allen said.
Bridget Bowman is a national political reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: A 20-year-old Amish woman with leukemia got measles and died in Pa.’s largest outbreak in three decades
articles.title_zh: A 20-year-old Amish woman with leukemia got measles and died in Pa.’s largest outbreak in three decades
articles.content_orig:
After measles swept through her household, the young woman wanted to get vaccinated. Her doctor said she couldn't because she had leukemia and the treatments had weakened her immune system.
The headstone had not yet been placed Thursday on the freshly dug grave where a 20-year-old Amish woman was buried this week amid the rolling clover fields and dairy farms at the edge of suburban Philadelphia.
Newly wed, and receiving treatment for blood cancer, she was the last of nine siblings sickened when measles swept through her unvaccinated family’s home on a one-lane road in Lancaster County.
At first, the home remedies that eased their symptoms seemed to help her, too: Soothing the fever with bath soaks. Calming the rash with coconut or olive oil. Cloistering in a dark room to ease light sensitivity.
Then her fever spiked. She struggled to breathe and had to sleep sitting up in a recliner in the living room, her maternal grandmother recalled.
Her family does not operate cars, in keeping with Amish beliefs, so they hired a driver to take her to the emergency department at Hershey Medical Center about an hour away. She died about two weeks later in the intensive care unit there, her grandmother said.
Speaking on the porch of her stone farmhouse, the grandmother described the family’s experience with Pennsylvania’s largest measles outbreak in three decades, now the nation’s largest. At her request, The Inquirer withheld her name and that of her deceased granddaughter to protect the family’s privacy.
She said her granddaughter ultimately developed double pneumonia and died after the family decided to discontinue use of a ventilator.
The cancer made her especially vulnerable to a virus as contagious as measles, which will infect 9 in 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed.
“Her immune system wasn’t built up,” the grandmother said. “She just couldn’t take it with the measles.”
Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday its fifth measles-related death , revealing only that the latest fatality was an unvaccinated Lancaster County resident. Health officials did not provide further details, citing privacy laws.
But it appears from the grandmother’s account, along with other records and news reports, that three of the five deaths occurred in adults with measles. Other reported deaths included an 18-year-old Amish woman from Mifflin County and a 40-year-old from Jefferson County with severe respiratory conditions. Two Amish infants in Lancaster County who had confirmed measles cases also died. All five cases involved people who were unvaccinated, either by choice or because they were too young to receive vaccines.
The number of deaths in adults is striking, said Paul Offit, who heads the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. Widespread childhood vaccinations had eradicated the disease in the United States, leaving mostly children too young to be vaccinated at high risk in recent decades. Now multiple generations of unvaccinated children are adults, exposing wider vulnerabilities across the state, Offit said.
“We’re aging out a population that was never vaccinated,” he said.
After learning the details of the 20-year-old’s death from The Inquirer, Offit explained that measles commonly leads to pneumonia.
“The measles virus reproduces itself in the lungs and can cause severe and occasionally fatal infection,” he said.
The young woman, the second oldest in a line of nine siblings, ages 6 to 22, feared getting measles in the outbreak in Lancaster County, her grandmother said.
About two years ago, she was diagnosed with leukemia, a blood cancer, and began medical treatment with the help of an “English” neighbor — as Amish call outsiders — to drive her to her medical appointments.
The treatment regimen of chemo and steroids further weakened her immune system. She knew she was at risk of more severe sickness from a viral infection like measles, which started spreading throughout her family in the late summer.
Her eight siblings, her parents, and her new husband all got sick, the grandmother said.
Along with home remedies, family members drank extra fluids to stay hydrated, the grandmother said.
“They weren’t worried,” the grandmother said. “ Measles just has to take its course.”
Although no one in the household was vaccinated, they are not opposed to the vaccine based on Amish beliefs. They believe it’s an individual choice, she said, and many Amish people opt not to get vaccinated because they “don’t know what’s in it.”
“We wouldn’t tell people not to get vaccinated,” the grandmother said. “It’s up to each person.”
As illness spread in her household, her granddaughter grew more worried about getting the virus than about the vaccine that medical authorities have long considered safe and effective.
She asked her doctor if she could get a measles vaccination. Her doctor said no. “She wasn’t allowed to get the shot because she was on chemo,” the grandmother said.
The measles vaccine contains a live but weakened virus, and her granddaughter was already immunocompromised from the leukemia treatment.
After getting measles, her granddaughter began to feel better in early September. She picked vegetables from the family’s garden to make soup using tomato juice as the broth. She canned jars for the coming cold months, her grandmother said.
“She had good days,” the grandmother said.

Then, in mid-September, she spiked a high fever, and her breathing became labored.
“She could hardly breath. Her lungs were just in bad shape,” she said.
The Amish typically only seek emergency hospital treatment until “sometimes we’re dying,” the grandmother said, recalling how her husband got chided by a doctor in 2018 for waiting too long to get the heart surgery he desperately needed.
“We do what we can at home,” she said. “We have so many natural things we can do.”
By Sept. 11, the family knew it was time to take her granddaughter for emergency care at Hershey Medical Center.
At Hershey’s ER, doctors gave her a chest X-Ray, but sent her home before reading it, the grandmother said.
“They wouldn’t do anything for her. They didn’t want her there,” she said. (A Hershey spokesperson did not reply to a request for comment on Friday.)
A Hershey provider later called and left a voicemail message asking the family to bring her back. Although the family has a phone in their house, the grandmother said they rarely use it. With the ringer off, all calls go to voicemail, she said.
A driver took them back to the hospital, where she was admitted on Sept. 14. An ultrasound showed fluid between the lining of her lungs and in her lungs. She was diagnosed with double pneumonia, her grandmother said.
Hospital staff hooked her up to supplemental oxygen.
“They had the oxygen up as far as they could and she still had to work to breathe,” the grandmother said.
About a week later, they moved her to the intensive care unit, where they sedated her so they could put her on a ventilator while intubated.
The hospital allowed two family members at a time to sit by her bed. Her granddaughter’s young husband and the girl’s mother sat vigil, the grandmother said.
As she continued to deteriorate, life support was the only remaining option, and it carried the risk of neurological complications, including brain death.
The family didn’t want that, the grandmother said. “They couldn’t do anything more,” she said.
They turned off the oxygen and shut off the ventilator, Family members, including her new husband’s parents, gathered around her bed.
She died with a breathing tube still in her mouth, the grandmother said.
More than 300 people came to the family’s home on Monday for the funeral service and viewing. She was buried in a cemetery near the family’s home, about a month before what would have been her first wedding anniversary.

articles.title_orig: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.title_zh: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.content_orig:
A nonprofit environmental group working with primates in Sebangau National Park says the dry peatlands can be a catalyst to more destruction.
(CN) â Since early August, wildfires have devastated the fragile rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, causing widespread toxic air across Indonesia. Itâs affected most communities in all parts of the region of Kalimantan, a part of the worldâs third largest island under Indonesiaâs governance.
The fires are fueled by shifting El NiÃ±o climate patterns, causing severe drought and extremely dry conditions in the islandâs peatlands, among the planetâs most effective carbon-capturing ecosystems and vital habitat for wildlife found nowhere else in the world.
Sebangau National Park in Central Kalimantan is home to an estimated 6,000 to 9,000 critically endangered Bornean orangutans, one of the islandâs largest populations. The nonprofit Borneo Nature Foundation said a fire crossed the park boundary for the first time in early September.
âOur teams pushed it back, and it was largely confined to sedge and open peat, but some reforestation sites are impacted,â Dr. Susan Cheyne, the Science Director for the Borneo Nature Foundation and the Vice Chair for the International Union for the Conservation of Nature special project group for small apes, said in an email to Courthouse News.
âOur priority is to keep fire out of the forest, because that protects every orangutan in it at once,â she said. Cheyne and her colleagues monitor and document conditions in Borneo, while volunteer firefighting crews work to keep fires out of orangutan habitat and nearby villages. Capturing and removing the apes is âa last resort,â Cheyne said.
Sebangau is also home to several of the worldâs rarest primates, including the largest known population of Bornean white-bearded gibbons, an ape Cheyne has studied for over 20 years.
Gibbons are known for their musical vocalizations, or âsongs.â Males sing alone in the morning before females join them in duets later in the day.
âDuring the 2006 fires I found that gibbons sang less often and sang shorter songs on smoky days. Their song is how they defend territory and keep pair bonds, so this matters,â said Cheyne. âA similar pattern has since been recorded in wild Bornean orangutans exposed to wildfire smoke.â
Gibbons rarely come to the ground, and fire survivors are often left in small, isolated forest patches with little food. Other primates, including red langurs and long-tailed and southern pig-tailed macaques, are found only in Southeast Asia, and each fire further reduces their numbers. Little is known about how fires affect nocturnal slow lorises and western tarsiers, Cheyne said.
The national park includes vast peat swamps, made of partly decomposed plant material accumulated over thousands of years. In parts of Sebangau, the peat dome reaches 12 meters deep.
Peatlands are naturally waterlogged, like giant sponges that do not burn. But in the 1990s and early 2000s, illegal loggers dug hundreds of canals to float timber out of the forest. Those canals continue draining the peat, causing it to dry out and become fuel.
âIn a long dry season like this one, a dried-out peat swamp is a tinderbox,â said Cheyne.
âWhat makes peat fires so hard to fight is that they burn downwards and sideways, not just across the surface. Fire smolders underground through the dry peat, sometimes for weeks, long after the flames above have gone out. These are sometimes called zombie fires.â
Peat fires are particularly dangerous because from the surface, a person may see nothing amiss, perhaps âjust a thin wisp of smoke,â Cheyne said, while a meter below the peat burns and can set nearby tree roots aflame, easily toppling them. And peat fires also produce dense, toxic smoke.
Cheyne said since 2015, the foundation and local crews have built over 1,000 dams to block drainage canals, planted almost a million trees, drilled hundreds of water boreholes and increased support for up to eight fire teams.
âThat preparation is why we are holding,â she said. But itâs still a tenuous situation. For the short-term, Cheyne said, the goal is to keep the firefighting teams in the field fed, equipped and safe, which costs about $100 a day per team. It also means investing in equipment, such as thermal drones that can detect underground peat fires and rewetting the peat, so it doesnât reignite. The foundation, she said, is actively seeking donations from international bodies, advocacy groups and concerned individuals.
While hotspots in Kalimantan have declined since the beginning of the month, according to the foundation, rains are not expected until late October or November.
âWe are not out of this yet,â said Cheyne.
Cheyne said Borneo Nature Foundation Internationalâs co-founder Simon Husson recently passed a troop of monkeys on a river trip and they moved through trees beside mile after mile of burned riverbank.
âThat is the picture,â she said. âLife hanging on right at the edge.â

articles.title_orig: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.title_zh: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.content_orig:
High school students face no shortage of challenges, from maintaining top grades to balancing extracurricular activities. But for Wayzata High School sophomore Aakya Manamperi, her pursuits extend far beyond the classroom. In fact, they stretch all the way across the globe.
Manamperi, 15, is a second-degree black belt and one of the nation’s top-ranked karate competitors in her age group.
Later this fall, she will travel to Spain to compete on the global stage at the World Karate Commission (WKC) World Championships.
Inside Dojo Karate in Medina, Manamperi serves as a patient instructor, guiding young students through fundamental martial arts skills. But don’t let her calm demeanor fool you. When she steps onto the tournament floor, she’s a force to be reckoned with.
“It’s kind of a really male-dominated sport,” Manamperi said. “So, being a female, and a female of color, it’s really important for me to go out there and represent.”
Aakya Manamperi teaches karate to a group of kids at Dojo Karate in Medina.
Manamperi began practicing karate at age 6. Achieving elite national status has required years of rigorous discipline and daily training.
“I’ve been training two hours every single day,” Manamperi said. “The first hour is mostly cardio, training drills, working on technique. And the second hour is just focusing on my kata that I’m going to be competing.”
Kata, her primary discipline, consists of detailed, high-intensity sequences of movements. Judges evaluate performance based on technique, power, rhythm, balance and presentation—an evaluation process that has earned Manamperi an impressive collection of trophies and medals over the years.
Her dedication has drawn praise from local mentors, including Dojo Karate Medina owner Javier Franco, who noted the positive influence she has on younger students.
“Of course, this is a big impact on the students,” Franco said. “They always see their instructors as their heroes.”
A collection of some of the awards Aakya Manamperi has received for her karate expertise.
Manamperi’s drive to make an impact extends beyond martial arts competition. Outside the dojo, she founded The Girl Shield Project , a student-led organization dedicated to empowering young women through self-defense training, leadership development and health education.
“We do online events, we do in-person events, and so far we’ve reached around 200 different girls in around 20 different countries, and hopefully growing to some more,” Manamperi said.
In addition to her athletic and community achievements, Manamperi maintains a 3.99 GPA at Wayzata High School, where she participates in Science Olympiad and Student Council.
As she prepares to represent the United States in Spain, the weight of her accomplishments is not lost on her.
“Honestly, I appreciate it so much,” Manamperi said. “It’s amazing for me to be able to share things that I like to do and my passions with the world and kind of compete in it. It’s something that I still pinch myself to this day about.”

The National Weather Service has issued an extreme heat warning for the greater Los Angeles area from Friday through at least next Thursday, and forecasters say it’ll likely extend beyond that.
Temperatures are expected to be in the mid-90s to mid-100s, even in coastal areas.
“Unfortunately, we don't really see an end to it as far as we can tell, and that's probably the biggest thing we wanna highlight, is that while we have had hotter events this season already, this one might be the longest-lasting,” said Ryan Kittell, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Kittell said they expect to see a few daily records to be broken.
Southern California saw a record-breaking 10-day heat wave in the summer of 2022 .
Forecasters say conditions likely won’t meet the threshold for issuing red flag warnings (extremely dry air and windy conditions), but the risk of fire is still going to be high during the heat wave.
“It’s still concerning, and if a fire were to get started in the wrong area, it could grow pretty fast,” Kittell said. “ We do have a history of large fires in similar environments with similar heat, similar time of the year.”
As of Thursday afternoon, Southern California Edison said nearly 10,000 customers in parts of Riverside County were under consideration for power shutoffs , which are used to reduce the risk of electrical equipment starting a fire.
In L.A., Orange, San Bernardino, and Riverside counties, call 3-1-1 or call for a list of cooling centers. In the city of Los Angeles, you can also find a list of recreation centers , senior centers and libraries — all good choices for cooling off — online.

Kittell said people should make plans to stay cool during the long heat wave, and check in on neighbors who are elderly, or on families with young children.
Officials say residents should limit outdoor activities to the early morning hours, stay in air-conditioned places in the afternoon and evening hours, and stay hydrated.

EL PASO — A judge on Friday blocked further border barrier construction in the Big Bend region, approving an environmental group’s motion for a preliminary injunction.
At the end of Friday’s hearing, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone asked the courtroom to remain calm while she read her order aloud from the bench. She ruled that the plaintiffs’ constitutional claims to halt the construction were likely to succeed and her preliminary injunction against “ground-distrurbing activities” would remain in effect while the suit continued to play out in court.
The legal team at the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group, filed the lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security and its secretary in April on behalf of the Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving a historic church in Presidio County, and Danny William Miller, a Rio Grande river guide and landowner who stands to lose his property in Redford to the wall.
The lawsuit argues that the five contracted border wall projects in the region are unconstitutional for a range of reasons, including violating the constitutional separation of powers and depriving citizens of their land.
The suit documents what could be lost to border barrier construction along the Rio Grande if it’s allowed to proceed. Zeynep Graves, a lawyer with the Center for Biological Diversity, said in her closing arguments that the impact of wall construction in the Big Bend affected the community at all levels.
“The harm reaches far beyond the landscape itself,” she said.
In emotional testimony, Miller compared the government building a wall across his property and blocking his access to the river to “a bullet to the head.”
Miller said once altered, the desert landscapes could never be replaced, and his work as a river guide would become “a tour of the military industrial complex, rather than a tour of the wilderness.”
Hudspeth County resident Bill Guerra-Addington testified that a border barrier would be a death sentence for his ranch on the Texas-Mexico border. “They’re taking the river away from us, and it’s devastating,” he said.
The government claims that physical border infrastructure is necessary, even in remote and lightly-trafficked areas like the Big Bend, to achieve what it calls “operational control” of the border –– zero unauthorized border crossings.
“Since the President took office, DHS has delivered the most secure border in history,” former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem wrote in a series of waivers that eased contracting laws across the entire southwest border. “More can be done, however.”
The Big Bend sector, which includes Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park, covers about a quarter of the length of the border but only sees between 1% and 3% of migrant apprehensions by U.S. Customs and Border Protection each year.
Since news of the government’s plans for border barriers in Big Bend broke in January 2026, a grassroots bipartisan backlash has formed across the region, slowly pushing the government to adjust its plans for physical border infrastructure — walls, roads, fences, lights, sensors and more — totaling over $7.5 billion in government contracts.
In response to the public outcry, DHS officials have countered with hypotheticals about what could happen in Big Bend if migrant traffic shifts in response to wall construction elsewhere along the southern border. CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott issued a statement that the agency’s goal was to protect the national park from future cartel activity.
Despite the scale of the opposition, contractors have been bulldozing new roads in the park after the government waived the Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Protection Act to support the “expeditious construction of barriers and roads” along the border.
So far, six lawsuits have been filed over the Big Bend wall. On Thursday, a judge rejected a request for a temporary restraining order in a different case that sought to halt work in and around Big Bend National Park, which had been paused through the month of September.

articles.title_orig: Ken Urker, Partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, Is Found Dead in Louisiana
articles.title_zh: Ken Urker, Partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, Is Found Dead in Louisiana
articles.content_orig:
Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s ex-husband Ryan Anderson expressed his “shock” after learning of the death of her former partner, Ken Urker.
Urker died from a suspected overdose at his Louisiana home Thursday, on his 34th birthday. He was found with drug paraphernalia and a gun at the time of his death, according to a police report obtained by Page Six.
“I didn’t believe it at first. I was like no. My initial thought was shock, like, ‘Hmm, how’d that happen?’” Anderson told “The Sarah Fraser Show” Friday.
Anderson, 40, said his thoughts quickly turned to Blanchard and Aurora, the 1-year-old daughter she shared with Urker.
“My immediate thought went to, ‘How’s Gypsy?’ My immediate thought was, ‘How’s she doing. And what about their kid?’” he continued.
Blanchard and Anderson married in June 2022 while she was serving time for her role in the 2015 murder of her mom, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard.
They announced their split in March 2024 after Blanchard was released from prison in December 2023.
Weeks later, Blanchard confirmed her relationship with Urker, whom she first met while she was incarcerated in 2017. They got engaged in October 2018 but later split.
After rekindling their romance in early 2024, Blanchard and Urker welcomed Aurora in December of that year .
Anderson said he and Urker “never really saw eye to eye,” though they never met face-to-face.
“We never met in person, but we had exchanges on the phone and we’ve had text messages. We’ve interacted and they were never good,” he said.
“But you still hate to hear that somebody passed away.”
Anderson revealed he has not spoken to Blanchard in about a year. He reached out to her dad, Rod Blanchard, after hearing the news.
“I said, ‘Hey, man, I’m hearing this news. If it’s true, tell Gypsy I’m sorry. Tell her I’m here for her if she needs me,’” he said.
“I was always somebody who could make her laugh when she was sad or give her comfort.”
Anderson said his “main concern is Aurora and Gypsy” and that he would be there for Blanchard as a friend if she reaches out.
“I don’t know if she will or not,” he added, “but if she does, I would be there for her strictly as just being there for her because I always was.”
Page Six earlier reported that Blanchard and Urker had quietly ended their relationship about a month before his death .
Blanchard claimed in a statement Friday that Urker died of a suspected overdose and said that she was “in disbelief .”
“I can’t think. I’ve screamed until my throat burns,” she said. “Ken was an amazing father and a man who was deeply loved. He will forever be my soulmate and my red string, a connection that time, distance, and even death can never erase.”
She also pointed to Urker’s struggles with negative comments aimed at him online.
“Ken endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit,” she said. “The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure.”

This week, Hillsborough County in Florida, which includes Tampa, declared a state of emergency linked to a growing number of dengue cases. So far this year, around 485 cases have been reported in the state , according to the CDC. The disease, which is transmitted by mosquitoes, can cause serious flu-like illness, and one person in Florida has died in the outbreak so far this year, the state’s department of health told media outlets in September.
Seasonal outbreaks of the disease, which affects up to 400 million people worldwide annually , are not unusual in Florida, and they’re often linked to travelers. But this time is a little different, says Michael Johansson, an epidemiologist at Northeastern University. “This is the most locally acquired cases that we've seen in the state,” he says.
Dengue, sometimes called dengue fever, is caused by a collection of viruses carried by mosquitoes , primarily Aedes aegypti . Dengue is endemic in a wide swath of the tropics, and usually, most Americans who have the infection acquire it outside of the U.S. during travel. Dengue symptoms can occur 5-7 days after being bitten and range from mild to severe. They may include painful body aches as well as fever and can last up to 10 days .
However, in parts of the U.S. where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes live, they can bite infected people and start to spread the disease locally. “The general pattern that we see—and we've seen this for more than a decade now—is that there are frequent travel-associated cases” in Florida, says Johansson. “We know we have the right vectors there, especially in southern Florida, where there's lots of Aedes aegypti, and there is some local transmission that occurs. Usually that looks like just one or two cases, but sometimes there are small outbreaks.”
In 2009, when two locally acquired infections were identified in Key West, public-health surveillance revealed that a substantial share of people in the town had markers in their blood showing a recent encounter with dengue , even if they hadn’t had symptoms. That suggests that in an outbreak, dengue is likely to be infecting more people than might immediately be clear from case counts.
One distinctive feature of dengue, however, is that the second time someone is infected is likely to be much worse than the first. Sometimes a second infection can progress to dengue hemorrhagic fever , which can involve bleeding and a drop in blood pressure, and is sometimes fatal.
This pattern, where the second exposure is more dangerous than the first, has complicated attempts to vaccinate people against the disease. In 2017, Sanofi Pasteur, the manufacturer of the dengue vaccine Dengvaxia, alerted the government of the Philippines that serious dengue infections might occur in people who had received the vaccine as their first exposure to the disease. No dengue vaccine is currently available in the U.S.; Dengvaxia was available starting in 2019 but in 2025 was discontinued by the manufacturer, which cited low demand.
So far, dengue has not established a permanent foothold in the continental U.S., says Johansson. There are a few reasons why that might be: large numbers of people in Florida, where Aedes aegypti thrive, stay within air-conditioned spaces when they’re most active, which means chains of transmission tend to be short.
And the mosquitoes themselves are not particularly adventurous. They tend to stay close to home, within about a 100-meter range, so “it takes people to move the virus around,” says Johansson. If someone who’s infected doesn’t travel, the virus doesn’t either.
There is no cure for dengue; the only treatments are for symptoms. If you are in an area with mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the best way to protect yourself is to avoid mosquito bites. Keep windows closed or use screens, cover as much of your skin as possible with clothing when outdoors, and use mosquito repellent, says Johansson.
Keep yards free of containers that could fill with water and serve as breeding zones for mosquitoes. You’ll have to be vigilant: “These mosquitoes in particular, they can breed in a plastic bag that's collected a little bit of rainwater,” says Johansson.
Cooler weather brings relief. “We're getting to the time of year when things are cooling down, so we should expect a decrease in transmission,” says Johansson. “However, it's still hot in Florida right now”—so it’s not time to drop your guard yet.

articles.title_orig: Russian-speaking Latvians who back Ukraine and value their language are heading into an election without an obvious political home
articles.title_zh: Russian-speaking Latvians who back Ukraine and value their language are heading into an election without an obvious political home
articles.content_orig:
Latvia will elect its 15th Saeima, or parliament, on October 3. September polls suggest seven political groups have a chance of winning seats. Two of them — the Sovereign Power / Young Latvians alliance and Latvia First — are competing vigorously to win over voters who once supported the “Russian” parties. Their rivalry is one of the campaign’s central stories: almost 35% of Latvian citizens speak Russian at home. Polls also suggest that the traditional “Russian” parties, especially Harmony Center, remain below the 5% threshold. Writing for Meduza, Sergejs Potapkins , a political scientist and researcher at the Latvian Institute of International Affairs, traces the complicated history of Latvia’s parties that have sought to represent Russian speakers.
In 2018, Harmony, the main party representing Latvia’s Russian-speaking voters, finished first in the parliamentary elections with 19.8% of the vote and 23 of the 100 seats. Four years later, it failed to clear the 5% threshold and lost its place in the Saeima. Aleksejs Rosļikovs ’ For Stability! party filled part of the vacuum, but by February 2026, its parliamentary faction had also broken up. Within a few years, the established system of political representation for Russian speakers had collapsed.
Ahead of the October 3, 2026, elections, the political landscape for “Russian votes” has become completely fragmented. Old names are returning to the ballot, politicians are moving between parties, and several political groups are vying for Harmony’s former electorate. Yet none has regained Harmony’s ability to unite very different people around the Russian language and the demand to protect their shared interests.
The history of the party model relying primarily on Russian votes began long before Harmony. After Latvia regained independence in 1991, disputes over citizenship, the Russian language, and the Soviet past became the main dividing lines between parties.
The groups described as “Russian” primarily represented Russian speakers, although their leaders and voters came from many different ethnic backgrounds. Only Latvian citizens had the right to vote in parliamentary and local elections. The Russian parties also defended noncitizens , who could not themselves vote for them.
Two distinct strands of Russian-speaking politics were already taking shape in the fifth Saeima, elected in 1993. Some groups sought from the outset to work within the restored Latvian state: the Harmony for Latvia, Revival for the Economy electoral list won 13 of the 100 seats. Its leader was Jānis Jurkāns , a Popular Front activist and independent Latvia’s first foreign minister. The other strand grew out of political resistance to the restoration of Latvian statehood. Equal Rights , which won seven seats, emerged from a Supreme Council faction of the same name, most of whose members had opposed the restoration of Latvia’s independence.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
From the outset, Russian-speaking political representation brought together people who had only recently stood on opposite sides of the central conflict over leaving the USSR and restoring independence.
These two visions of the future of Russians in Latvia led to fragmentation in the 1995 elections for the sixth Saeima. Jurkāns’ National Harmony Party, formed a year earlier from the former alliance, argued for integrating Russian speakers. The Socialist Party’s electoral list, which included Equal Rights, presented itself as their defender and appealed to voters by defining itself in opposition to the state. Together, the parties won 11 seats, down from 20. Their position had weakened, but continuing public disputes over citizenship and language only increased demand for political representation for Russian speakers.
The response was the For Human Rights in a United Latvia alliance, known by its Russian acronym, ZaPChEL. Ahead of the 1998 elections for the seventh Saeima, the National Harmony Party, Equal Rights, and the socialists formed its core. The small Russian Party also joined. Registration problems forced the bloc to run under the National Harmony Party’s name; it won 16 seats. ZaPChEL managed to unite liberal centrists with socialists: Russian speakers’ rights proved more important than ideological differences.
In the elections for the eighth Saeima, ZaPChEL finished second and won 25 seats, just one fewer than the winner. That success sharpened disagreements over whether it was possible to form a government with Alfrēds Rubiks’ socialists and Tatjana Ždanoka’s Equal Rights, which had once opposed the restoration of independence. Ethnic Latvian parties still considered ZaPChEL an unacceptable partner and refused to form a coalition with it. As a result, the National Harmony Party left ZaPChEL in 2003.
In 2005, the party became a founding member of the Harmony Center alliance. In 2010, it joined New Center and the Social Democratic Party to form Harmony. ZaPChEL later also became a single party and renamed itself the Latvian Russian Union in 2014.
Harmony inherited many of ZaPChEL’s members and much of its experience. It brought the broad alliance’s political base back together while presenting a more moderate image. It sought to move beyond being an ethnic party and become a broader social democratic party capable of forming a governing coalition and finding common ground with the ethnic Latvian majority. The Latvian Russian Union, by contrast, remained focused on defending minorities, emphasizing language, schools, noncitizens, and resistance to assimilation.
The Harmony Center alliance finished first in the 2011 elections; the reorganized Harmony party did so in 2014 and 2018 . But neither the alliance nor the party ever entered the national government. Ethnic Latvian political groups formed majority coalitions without it. This was Harmony’s central tragedy — even when it won an election, it was doomed to remain in opposition.
For potential partners, disagreements over history and language remained an obstacle — above all, Harmony’s reluctance to acknowledge the Soviet occupation of Latvia explicitly and its equivocal position on recognizing Latvian as the sole official language. There was also distrust of the party’s ties to Moscow following the cooperation agreement it signed with United Russia in 2009.
That isolation created the central paradox: Harmony could explain its lack of results by saying that others were unwilling to let Russian speakers into government. But after several election cycles, questions arose about what another victory would achieve. The party won votes, secured the largest parliamentary faction, and found itself isolated again. Repeated victories brought it no closer to joining the government, and its leaders increasingly faced accusations that they were not taking power because they were comfortable remaining in opposition.
Everything changed in 2009, when Harmony chairman Nils Ušakovs won power in Riga. The party could now show voters tangible results at the city level: free public transportation for pensioners and schoolchildren

articles.title_orig: University of Lynchburg AI Garage prepares business students to solve real-world problems with agentic AI
articles.title_zh: University of Lynchburg AI Garage prepares business students to solve real-world problems with agentic AI
articles.content_orig:
The rapidly expanding capabilities and applications of AI has created a new frontier in higher education. As it is more widely integrated into industry and becoming a highly desired skill, universities are faced with finding effective and ethical ways of teaching the technology and preparing their students for a more technologically savvy workplace.
“Our students are going out into the workplace, and they’re entering a bit of a storm,” said Price Jett, University of Lynchburg’s chief financial officer.
“AI is the highest impacting tool set that we can use to give lifts to businesses. … But it dawned on me that our students are ill prepared, and maybe even some of our professors [are] unaware of what’s going on. … So, we came up with this concept called the [AI] Garage.”
The AI Garage is an agentic AI laboratory where selected students can experiment with building AI agents to solve a company’s real business problems. Jett and Dr. Timothy Schauer, dean of the School of Professional and Applied Sciences, launched the AI Garage as an experiment in the Spring of 2026.
The project brought together businesses, students, and industry experts who Schauer and Jett referred to as “thought accelerators.”
“We talk about ethics — we talk about responsibility — but this isn’t just basic AI where you’re using it to write your papers for you,” said Schauer. “We want it to accomplish things that can be done behind the scenes so that the human doesn’t have to do it, but still stays in the loop.”
Agentic AI goes beyond the generative large language models, such as ChatGPT or Gemini, which typically create content in response to a prompt. Given a goal, an AI agent can determine the necessary steps, use connected tools, and perform tasks independently within defined rules, without requiring a new prompt at every stage. Depending on its purpose and permissions, an agent could analyze data, research information, send emails, schedule meetings, update records, or monitor a process and adjust its actions until the goal is met, all with a “persistent” memory capability similar to a human co-worker.
Of the nearly 30 students who showed interest in joining the pilot cohort, only seven were selected. Working in teams, the students spent four weeks at the end of the spring semester creating solutions to the real-world problems provided to them by four business executives.
The AI Garage was set up in Schewel Hall on special computers that were not connected to the University’s network. Schauer and Jett worked closely with Lynchburg’s IT department when setting up the lab to create a “walled garden” where the students would be able to safely work with their AI agents.
The students selected for the Garage had to be dedicated to the work, willing to put in the necessary time and effort even while finishing their course work and preparing for final exams and projects.
“These students were in this room — they ate there, some of them slept there,” said Schauer. “We’d come in in the morning, sometimes they worked all night. They were there on the weekends. They were very motivated.”
One of these students was Kristofer Hickson ʼ26, a veteran who transferred to Lynchburg after completing his associate degree at Central Virginia Community College.
“I’m not a computer science person,” said Hickson, a business major. “I have trouble finding my way around my own email. … [but] I can stumble my way around things and find my way into it.”
Hickson began experimenting with generative AI as he searched for work, using large language models, or LLMs, to refine and improve his resumes and cover letters so they better aligned with a given job description. Over time he became exhausted with manually prompting the LLM to do this work so he asked it to create a program that would do it automatically and upload and export to a file on his computer.
A few months before the AI Garage was launched, Hickson explained what he had been doing to Dr. Eric Kyper, a professor of business and economics. Kyper recognized that Hickson had stumbled into agentic AI and through their conversation, Hickson began thinking about what pursuing agentic AI could mean for his future.
Khurshid Kazimi ʼ28, an accounting major, was another student in the first AI Garage cohort. When she learned about the project, she immediately jumped at the opportunity.
“The first two weeks of working on building the AI agent was so difficult,” said Kazimi, an international student from Afghanistan. “And one thing that I realized later was that Price Jett and Dr. Schauer — they were not sharing all the information with us. … We were completely lost.”
Kazimi explained that Schauer and Jett wanted the students to take initiative and have the curiosity to figure out the next steps on their own. She was appreciative of the approach they took, saying, “They did the absolute best thing.”
She was also appreciative of her fellow students and the various talents each brought to the AI Garage.
“When we’re working together, we can find out the things that we cannot find out when we’re working alone,” Kazimi said.
“We were working on the same thing [and] I was not realizing a problem,” she explained. “I didn’t have that mindset to look at the problem in the same way … and then my teammate — she was finding out the thing that I couldn’t.”
At the end of the four-week period, the students presented their work to executives from each company. All of the companies involved wanted to use the tools the students created for them.
“The goal was not to give something valuable to a company, although that happened,” said Jett. “The goal [was] to teach our students how to solve business problems and give lift to businesses. That’s what businesses expect from us at the University.
“I think that’s our responsibility as leaders at the University to do that.”
Schauer added, “I do think that those universities that teach [AI] responsibly will put their students in a better position to actually get jobs and create value for companies. You can’t ignore that.”
Three students, including Hickson and Kazimi, were immediately offered internships or full-time employment.
“[Companies] don’t want people with computer science degrees,” said Hickson. “They want people with accounting skills, business skills, marketing skills, who know how to use agentic AI.”
He added, “I got a lot of confidence because [of] everything I built from scratch in the [AI] Garage. … It got me where I’m at and has helped give me the confidence to tread a little further.”
Schauer and Jett are now running the second round of the AI Garage this semester with four new businesses. For more information about the AI Garage, contact Schauer at [email protected] .
