articles.title_orig: ‘Maxi merde’: French presidential campaign rattled by a week of chaos
articles.title_zh: ‘Maxi merde’: French presidential campaign rattled by a week of chaos
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — French schools are getting torched. The far right’s brightest star is fighting for his political life after being accused of antisemitic remarks. And economic indicators are flashing bright red to warn of a potential sovereign debt disaster in the country.
The crises that have rocked France in recent days are exacerbating partisan cleavages in the country’s increasingly no-holds-barred presidential campaign.
In the words of one government adviser: “It’s the maxi merde .”
Though that individual, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the current situation, was only referring to the increasingly violent demonstrations outside secondary schools and the government’s slow-footed response to them, it’s a sentiment likely shared by French voters after a week of particularly bleak headlines.
If there are political winners, it’s not immediately clear who they are. Establishment candidates and moderate voices are still struggling to seize the narrative from far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen and her surging far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon — both of whom want to fundamentally reshape France and its relationship with Europe.
A survey by pollster Odoxa this week found that the French disapprove of the government’s handling of the student school protests, but they also disapprove of Mélenchon and his far-left party France Unbowed’s involvement.
Mélenchon’s allies have joined demonstrators outside schools, saying they were there to show support and protect minors from confrontations with police. But the government and France Unbowed’s political opponents accuse them of fanning the flames of violence — allegations they deny.
“There’s a battle over the narrative” between the political extremes, a Socialist Party adviser said.
Whatever the case, the week’s crises are showing just how nasty the campaign can get with two populist candidates unafraid to stoke partisan divisions leading the polls.
The French government has tried to get a grip on the unravelling protests, holding a crisis meeting Thursday and meeting youth representatives on Friday.
“Lecornu is always running behind the crises, he’s always reacting,” said a centrist adviser.
Le Pen, however, blamed agitators for stirring up violence at the protests and accused France Unbowed of “giving a helping hand” to “agents of chaos and insurrection.”
For her National Rally party, the crisis is a useful opportunity to try to convince voters that her party is the best choice for those concerned with public safety.
“We have a government that is incapable of maintaining public order and a left that is stoking the fire,” said National Rally MP Laurent Jacobelli in an interview with POLITICO.
“We are the only legitimate ones when it comes to [security],” he added.
But the unrest is also a useful distraction for Le Pen as her party president and heir apparent, Jordan Bardella, tries to bat down allegations published Monday by investigative outlet Mediapart that he sent antisemitic messages on Facebook Messenger when he was a 17-year-old activist.
Bardella vehemently denied the allegations and vowed to sue Mediapart, but the website on Thursday published another story outlining how it verified the claims, which included screenshots and conversation data downloaded directly from Meta with the help of their sources.
Bardella was tipped to become Le Pen’s prime minister if she came to power, but his future appears to hang on a thread.
“Do we need to unplug him? It’s Marine’s decision,” said a National Rally elected representative. “It all depends on whether the proof is serious.”
But Bardella is no small player, and the National Rally’s opponents are hoping that the fallout of his possible resignation would damage Le Pen’s campaign durably.
All of this comes just hours after Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s minority government introduced a 2027 budget with €43 billion worth of savings designed to reassure markets fretting about France’s massive debt and a stubbornly high budget deficit.
But without a parliamentary majority, getting lawmakers to agree to painful cuts will be tough, even if the specter of a potential financial crisis is starting to loom large.
Borrowing cost have reached their highest levels since 2008 and the spread between French 10-year bonds and German ones — an indicator that measures investors’ appetite to hold French debt over more traditionally stable German debt — shot above 150 basis points on Friday, a level not seen in years.
One lawmaker from President Emmanuel Macron’s party Renaissance said he doesn’t see how the presidential hopefuls from the political center — former PMs Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal — will be spared the fallout.
“Every minute spent on the budget is a minute spent staring at our incapacity to get ourselves out of the mess,” the MP said.
Meanwhile, Mélenchon has called for his party officials to join more protests planned next Tuesday and protect pupils against alleged police violence. That could propel him to center stage, but it could also backfire if he is seen as taking part in the unrest.
Centrist MEP Sandro Gozi said the allegations against Bardella and the far left’s attitude to the protests “complicate the normalization strategy of the two sides.”
“Both Le Pen and Mélenchon are extremists who are far from fundamental Republican and European values,” Gozi said.
But as Macron’s term winds down, a sense is taking hold that France has been mismanaged and that parts of the country are falling apart.
It’s a perception any would-be successor with links to the current president will struggle to combat on the campaign trail.
Elisa Bertholomey and Sarah Paillou contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s midnight spy satellite launch quietly set a new record
articles.content_orig:
Falcon Heavy launched its first NRO mission while SpaceX landed four boosters in one day.
SpaceX closed out one of its busiest days ever with a midnight Falcon Heavy launch from Florida, and the rocket’s two side boosters came home to finish off a landing record the company had never set before.
Falcon Heavy lifted off from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at 11:54 p.m. ET Thursday carrying NROL-97, a classified payload for the National Reconnaissance Office. It was the first time the NRO has flown on Falcon Heavy after 22 missions on Falcon 9, and the first NRO mission bought through the National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 2 contract awarded in 2025, according to Spaceflight Now .
Falcon Heavy lifts off from pad 39A in Florida for the 14th time! pic.twitter.com/uuZLKNTdD7
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 2, 2026
Roughly eight minutes after liftoff, side boosters B1104 and B1072 touched down at Landing Zones 1 and 2 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, setting off double sonic booms across Brevard County. B1104 was flying for the second time and B1072 for the fourth. Both last flew on August 30 on NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, making NROL-97 the quickest turnaround between Falcon Heavy missions to date. The brand new center core, B1106, was expended in the Atlantic so the payload could reach its high energy orbit, and SpaceX’s mission page noted the fairing had previously flown on the NROL-95 mission in July.
The two landings capped a record for SpaceX. Earlier Thursday, Falcon 9 booster B1101 returned to Landing Zone 40 after sending the Crew-13 astronauts to the International Space Station , and another Falcon 9 launched the Transporter-18 rideshare with 130 payloads from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Spaceflight Now reported it was the first time SpaceX has landed four boosters in a single day, wrapping up the triple header Teslarati previewed on Wednesday .
Falcon Heavy’s side boosters land on LZ-1 and LZ-2 pic.twitter.com/dBPcNeggFx
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 2, 2026
The mission also brought Landing Zone 1 back for what may be its final landing. SpaceX first landed an orbital class booster there in December 2015, but its lease on the former Launch Complex 13 site ended in 2025 as the company moved Florida landings to new pads at its own launch complexes. With LZ-40 already holding the Crew-13 booster, SpaceX brought LZ-1 back into service for one more night. Launch tracker Next Spaceflight listed NROL-97 as the final expected landing at the site.
NROL-97 adds to a fast growing stack of national security work for SpaceX. The company has flown four Space Force missions from Vandenberg since mid August, several believed to carry Starshield satellites, pushing its Pentagon contract total for 2026 past $8 billion . Elon Musk was also named this week to help lead the Pentagon’s Project Meridian study on the future of warfare.
The Florida doubleheader stood out for another reason. The Space Coast saw only one launch in all of September as SpaceX shifts more of its East Coast infrastructure toward Starship, which reached orbit for the first time on Flight 14 just three days earlier.

Tesla’s Halloween teaser hides a covered vehicle and an Optimus hand rising from the ground.
Tesla has started teasing a Halloween software update for its vehicles, with  a short clip on X that reads, “Halloween is coming.” The clip opens on a glowing pumpkin before pulling back to the car’s center touchscreen, where the usual parked visualization has been replaced by a graveyard scene, and the vehicle draped with a white sheet so it reads as a cartoon ghost.
Halloween is coming pic.twitter.com/lM3ASUeOqX
— Tesla (@Tesla) October 1, 2026
The second detail is a robotic hand clawing its way out of the dirt like a zombie, which looks to be the hand of Tesla’s latest Optimus V3 humanoid robot. While Tesla still has not formally shown Optimus Gen 3 walking around in service, renders pulled from Tesla’s Android app last month gave the clearest look yet, including far more refined hands that Tesla has said carry 22 degrees of freedom. The hand has been the hardest part of the program. Musk has called it the majority of the robot’s engineering difficulty, and Tesla’s patents describe a design driven by tendons with the actuators moved into the forearm.
Tesla Optimus V3 hand and arm details revealed in new patents
Optimus also has a Halloween track record. Last October the robot handed out candy in Times Square , and a costumed “zombie” Optimus shuffled around the Tesla Diner in Los Angeles on Halloween night.
On the software side, Tesla’s 2025 Holiday Update expanded Santa Mode with a Santa sleigh, snowmen, snow effects, and a festive lock chime, so it wouldn’t be too far fetched if we saw something similar but themed for a  Halloween Mode.
Tesla Full Self-Driving is set to receive improvements to address its two biggest issues, according to a company engineer.
Director of Engineering at Tesla AI, Phil Duan, revealed in a post on X that improvements to both pothole avoidance and navigation “are coming,’ something we have heard many times in the past. However, there are a few things that seem to hint that things might be different this time around.
Improvements on both are coming.
— Phil Duan (@pduan) October 1, 2026
Pothole avoidance, navigation, speed control, and left lane camping are some of the most prevalent and frequently mentioned shortcomings of the Full Self-Driving suite. These are a few of the biggest issues that have kept Tesla Full Self-Driving as a Supervised suite, meaning drivers must remain attentive during operation .
Pothole avoidance was first mentioned as an “Upcoming Improvement” with the Tesla Full Self-Driving v14.3 update back in early April of this year. It was listed alongside “Expand reasoning to all behaviors beyond destination handling.”
Tesla is fixing Full Self-Driving’s pothole problem
It’s been six months since we first saw pothole avoidance explicitly mentioned , and it has not moved beyond that and joined the main release notes yet.
Tesla has not shed any light on why pothole avoidance has been such an issue for it to solve, but it also has issues identifying large bumps much of the time, so its modeling of sudden changes in road conditions is likely pretty weak at this particular point. I’ve had more issues with large bumps than potholes, personally, but both are issues that need to be resolved.
This is that big bounce that I mentioned in the quoted post.
It’s just a tad too drastic to take at the speed FSD wants to go over it. You can see me quickly swipe down into Sloth, but I intervened. https://t.co/K20PK9ysBg pic.twitter.com/81Oc82ZJcZ
— TESLARATI (@Teslarati) August 2, 2026
It makes sense that things might be pretty close to being released to the public, as we are going on such an extensive period of time between it being mentioned and it actually being deployed.
Navigation is likely the most painful part of using Full Self-Driving , as it routinely takes strange routes, has trouble with local rules (like Except Right Turn Stop Signs in Pennsylvania), and sometimes does not realize that maneuvers it is suggesting are against the law. Turning out of my neighborhood, you cannot turn left, yet my Model Y still suggests it roughly 70 percent of the time when I’m leaving.
However, Tesla might be close to a breakthrough on this . With the Summer Update, Tesla added “Preferred Routes” alongside “Automatic Navigation.”

articles.title_orig: Look up: Saturn is at its brightest this weekend
articles.title_zh: Look up: Saturn is at its brightest this weekend
articles.content_orig:
Saturn is at its biggest and brightest as the ringed planet reaches opposition this weekend.
Opposition happens as Earth passes between Saturn and the Sun, bringing the planet to its closest point to Earth for the year, about 784 million miles (1.26 billion km) away. This minimum distance makes Saturn appear brighter than at any other time this year.
Opposition is a great time to observe Saturn because it rises in the east around sunset, reaches its highest point around midnight, and remains visible through dawn. It will appear as a yellowish point of light in the eastern and southeastern sky.
You do not need a telescope to see Saturn, but even a small telescope can reveal the planet's rings and the brightest couple of its 293 moons. While you are spotting Saturn, look a bit higher for a large grouping of four stars astronomers call the Great Square of Pegasus. Up and to the right is the Circlet (ring) of Pisces. These are asterisms, or recognizable patterns within the more official constellations of Pegasus (the winged horse) and Pisces (the fish).
2026's view is very different from last year's when Earth crossed the plane of Saturn’s rings. Though the ring system spans about 175,000 miles, it is, on average, about 30 feet thick, so it effectively disappears when viewed edge-on. Since opposition in 2025, the rings are tilted 7.5 degrees from our perspective, bringing them back into view.
Saturn will be at opposition on Sunday morning at 8:21 a.m., but with clouds expected this weekend, the best views will be tonight, Friday, Oct. 2. The planet will remain an excellent evening target for much of the month.
Saturn’s last opposition occurred Sept. 21, 2025. Saturn reaches opposition every 378 days, or about two weeks later each year, as Earth catches up with Saturn in its orbit. We'll have similar good opportunities to view Jupiter as it reaches its own opposition on Feb. 11, 2027, followed by Mars on Feb. 19, 2027.

articles.title_orig: The world’s 10 most stress-free destinations
articles.title_zh: The world’s 10 most stress-free destinations
articles.content_orig:
Emma is a freelance travel journalist and long-standing contributor to The Telegraph. She is the recipient of several writing awards and has twice been named BGTW Travel Writer of the Year. She has spoken as a travel expert at the Royal Geographical Society, the Frontline Club and National Geographic headquarters in Washington DC and her Scottish lilt can occasionally be heard on the BBC’s From Our Own Correspondent. She can be contacted via Instagram at @emmathomsontravels
Emails. Phone calls. Appointments. Passwords. Protein. Water. Eight hours of sleep. Our lives have become a relentless pursuit of doing – and doing everything better. Even travelling can become a to-do list of bucket-list experiences, country counts and “Instagrammable” moments.
The antidote? The (admittedly laughably named) “stillcation” – a new way of holidaying that pushes back against our culture of constant productivity and self-improvement.
It’s not necessarily yoga at sunrise or a silent meditation retreat, although it can be. More simply, it’s about the absence of agenda. Of stripping life back to its essentials: good food, beautiful views, fresh air and anchoring yourself in the present moment. Instead of seeking destinations that offer the most to do, it asks where offers the best conditions for doing less.
“Man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone” was, according to French philosopher Blaise Pascal, the source of all humanity’s problems. Four centuries later, his observation feels oddly prescient. We are rarely sitting still – even when on holiday.
The constant pressure to optimise our lives can lead to chronic dysregulation of the nervous system, says Jamie Clements, a wellness retreat facilitator and author of the upcoming book The Next Breath . “Stress has become the baseline, and calm feels like the exception.”
Tour operators are catching onto our increasing thirst for deeper ways to unplug. Inghams recently ranked almost 100 European destinations according to their “stillest”, with criteria including walking trails per square kilometre, air quality, birdsong richness, stargazing quality, human density and forest cover (Scotland’s Wester Ross, see below, took the top spot).
Black Tomato is designing itineraries centred around themes such as “The Gift of Boredom” and “Sonic Sanctuaries”, with quiet-hour museum slots and low-stimulation dining. We’ve also seen a proliferation of Unplugged detox cabins and AirBnbs offering Wi-Fi and technology-free countryside boltholes.
Slowing down switches our nervous system from a fight-or-flight sympathetic state to a rest-and-digest parasympathetic system that lowers blood pressure and improves concentration by possibly stimulating neurogenesis – the creation of new brain cells.
But don’t assume that a stillcation will immediately evoke a state of inward zen. Like any other holiday – where it can take a week to unwind – the first day or two can feel uncomfortable.
The point of a stillcation isn’t simply that sitting around feels nice. Removing the constant demand for attention – and replacing the thrum of traffic, screens and notifications with wind, water, birdsong and walking – may create the conditions in which both mind and body can begin to really recover.
And the benefits extend beyond our own wellbeing. Several of the qualities that make a destination “still” – low population density, dark skies, forests, clean air, biodiversity and quiet trails – are also qualities that depend on healthy, protected environments.
Perhaps that is the real appeal of the stillcation. It doesn’t ask us to abandon movement, curiosity or adventure. It simply changes the objective. Travel becomes less about collecting experiences and more about noticing where we are; less about escaping life and more about inhabiting it. In a culture that has turned even rest into something to optimise, doing nothing might be the most radical itinerary of all.
Lungfuls of salty Cornish coastal air, strolls along the South West Coast Path and its secluded beaches, plus one of the UK’s last remaining temperate rainforests make this the ideal space to slow down.
How to do it: Jamie Clements offers a four-day breathwork retreat at Cabilla in Cornwall from £1,250 per person.
Wester Ross – in the remote north-west highlands of Scotland – is an unspoilt mash of moorlands and mountains that is home to pine martens, otters and the elusive wild cat. Its minimal light pollution creates star-rich dark skies.
How to do it: Wildlife Worldwide offer a six-day The Splendours of Wester Ross tour from £1,295 per person.
Glimpse magic in this Swedish Lapland village that’s probably one of the best places on Earth to see the northern lights (September–April) due to its cloud-free “blue hole”.
How to do it: Arctic Direct offer a three-night Abisko tour from £1,795 per person, including flights and activities.
Creating a wrinkled border between France and Spain, the bird-rich Pyrenees are scarce on people and big on open spaces for mindful hiking, yoga and thermal spas to unwind.
How to do it: Much Better Adventures offer a six-night Hike and Wild Swim in the French Pyrenees tour from £1,688 per person, excluding flights.
Switzerland’s “secret valley” is scattered with lö da ler (wooden cabins with books and reading benches), mindful running trails and forest bathing opportunities, including the Senda Botanica – a narrow path through 30 species of trees.
How to do it: Inntravel offer a seven-night Walking and Wildflowers in the Engadine Valley guided tour from £2,086 per person, excluding flights.
Described as one of the last pristine wilderness areas left on Earth, Yukon has a population of about 48,000 people spread across a territory roughly the size of Spain. It offers an extraordinary sense of space for hiking, wildlife watching, paddling and simply being outdoors.
How to do it: Canadian Sky offer a 10-night In the Footsteps of the Yukon Pioneers self-drive tour from £2,069 per person, including flights.
New Zealand ranks second in the world for peacefulness, behind Iceland. Pick the South Island’s Fiordland, Glenorchy and wild West Coast for vast mountains, sparse settlements and trails where the only itinerary is to walk, breathe and look.
How to do it: Pure Pods has off-grid glass cabins scattered across New Zealand from £240 per night.
Mountain trails, monasteries lit by butter lamps and a deliberately low-volume tourism model make Bhutan in south Asia particularly well suited to a holiday centred on contemplation rather than consumption.
How to do it: Raven Tours offer a nine-day Yoga, Culture and Stillness in the Kingdom of Happiness tour from £2,676 per person based on two sharing.
Nowhere serves up remote stillness quite like Torres del Paine National Park. A raw jostle of glacial lakes, mountains and clear air, it is ideal for forest bathing and restorative walking.
How to do it: Chile Nativo offer a five-day Torres del Paine Wellness Retreat from £1,700 per person from October to April, excluding flights.
One of the world’s least densely populated countries, Namibia in southern Africa is home to the oldest desert in the world, exceptionally dark skies and remarkable wildlife. Don’t miss Sossusvlei, Damaraland and the stark Skeleton Coast.
How to do it: Expert Africa offer a 14-day Discover Namibia self-drive safari from £4,220 per person based on two sharing.

articles.title_orig: How to rule the world: The book review no one asked for
articles.title_zh: How to rule the world: The book review no one asked for
articles.content_orig:
I am not smart enough to rule the world — though, it's important to note that I was planning to. I did not walk into my high school guidance counselor's office, crumple up the state-school brochures, and proclaim I wanted to be a dictator, but I liked having the option. Tragically, this backup plan was crushed when I read Theo Baker’s “How to Rule the World.”
My mother strong-armed this book into my life, proclaiming I would identify with the author.
Like any 19-year-old, I ignored this recommendation, creating a multi-month argument with my parent for no apparent reason. I finally made it around to reading the book between my busy summer schedule of rewatching trashy TV and staring at a wall, only to immediately read that the author I was supposed to be so similar to was a self-described nerd. Thanks, Mom; love you too.
I went into the book with absolutely no context, because I refused to read the jacket as a form of protest. The worst part of the book was… I actually liked it. Not just liked; I loved it to the point I became one of those pretentious people who bring a hard-cover book to appointments, coffee shops, even a tennis match. I was just waiting for someone to ask those magic words, "What are you reading?” What had become of me? The last book I read had watercolor rabbits on the cover. They say drugs are a gateway to a life of disaster; I argue this book set me on a worse track… I was a reader!
You may be asking yourself, “Wow, for a book review I have no clue what this book is actually about.” Well, that's why this article is in the humor section, and why I have not been promoted to culture. I am far too self-centered for ethical journalism. Which, ironically, is what the book is about.
Theo Baker was the student journalist who broke the story that led to Stanford President Marc Tessier-Lavigne's resignation. Baker published “How to Rule the World,” documenting the investigative process that exposed Lavigne's falsified scientific reports and uncovered the toxic symbiotic relationship between Stanford's elite students and Silicon Valley's aggressive venture capitalists.
His investigative journalism earned him the George Polk Award, making him the youngest recipient ever at just 18. I would like to take a moment for that to sink in. He was only a freshman. When I was a freshman, I was just trying to figure out how to do my laundry. I was definitely not cracking the core of our nation's problems with capitalism. I mean, it was on my to-do list, but I just never got around to it.
If, for some reason, you are reading this, Theo Baker, I mean, why wouldn't you be? I'm positive The Miami Student has a national foothold. Just know, the high-achieving STEM parents of the world (my mother) see you as their surrogate successful child when their kid decides to go down the dark path of wanting to be a comedian.
I could go more in-depth on the book's discussion of the intricacies of venture capital in the tech industry and Big Pharma, but I honestly was not smart enough to understand it all and would probably get sued for libel. I will say, to all the young people trying to find their place morally, intellectually, and socially: “How to Rule the World” is an incredibly motivating story urging Gen Z to go past their societal constraints to achieve their goals while striving to create a better, more truthful world. And to President Crawford, don’t worry, I am definitely not clever enough to be an investigative journalist!
Who in the newsroom wants to talk about organic chemistry? Carley would love to.
Mia loves the environment and will do anything to help it flourish. Although, there was this one time...
Cupcake games are awesome... but not for the team that is the cupcake.

articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Haitians remain in the grip of lethal gang violence as it continues to “adapt and expand”, the UN’s top rights official, Volker Türk, said on Friday.
In an update to the Human Rights Council , the High Commissioner welcomed the first Gang Suppression Force operations, mandated by the UN Security Council .
These will help boost security in Haiti “but the Force remains far below the strength needed”, Mr. Türk insisted, in support of its “full, accelerated deployment” with human rights safeguards embedded.
At least 5,700 people have been confirmed killed or injured by gangs – or during operations against them – since 1 January, according to the UN human rights office, OHCHR .
Gang members have also kidnapped more than 230 people and raped at least 1,000 women and girls. The real figures are likely much higher, Mr. Türk said.
In his update, the High Commissioner for Human Rights also warned that “extortion, looting and destruction of property” are crippling economic activity in Haiti.
The “constant danger” prevents people from reaching schools, hospitals, and essential services, Mr. Türk stressed.
Three hijacked ships have been freed after months in captivity, but five seafarers died during the rescue of one of them, the head of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has said.
IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez offered his condolences after the operation to free the HONOUR 25 in Somali waters on 29 September, in which several other crew members were seriously injured.
Mr. Dominguez said seafarers “should not have to lose their lives for the service they provide for the world”, and called for renewed resolve, targeted cooperation and the resources needed to stop piracy in the region.
The HONOUR 25 was one of three vessels released this week, along with the SEAMULL (also known as SIBU 1) and the MT EUREKA, all seized between April and August by pirates and armed robbers.
In total, 44 seafarers were freed and their governments are working to arrange their repatriation. Mr. Dominguez thanked Somalia's Government for its efforts, but noted that 22 seafarers remain captive aboard the ASANA.
He urged Governments to bring new initiatives, such as the proposed Group of Friends of Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, to the IMO, and stressed the importance of the EUNAVFOR Aspides and Atalanta operations for maritime security in the region.
An additional 11.7 million women and girls in 28 countries could face food insecurity by the end of the year due to the escalating conflict in the Middle East and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
These crises are driving up food prices and putting a strain on livelihoods and household resources, UN Women said in new analysis published on Friday.
Presenting the findings to journalists in Geneva, UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said the estimates are a potential scenario, not a forecast, and that the number is in addition to the 208 million women and girls who were already estimated to be food insecure or malnourished in these countries.
“Experience from past conflicts shows that when food is scarce, women often reduce the amount they eat or skip meals so that children and other family members can eat,” she said.
The greatest numbers of women and girls at risk are in populous countries, while South Sudan, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen and Palestine face the highest concentration of overlapping vulnerabilities.
UN Women recommends linking food and cash assistance to nutrition, protection, employment and agricultural services. Women should also have access to land, credit and productive resources.
The agency also highlighted the need for better collection of data that shows where food insecurity is worsening and who is eating less, losing income and carrying the heaviest burden of unpaid care work.

articles.title_orig: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.title_zh: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.content_orig:
Gino has proudly served the Tonawanda community from 351 Fries Road since opening his doors in 1983.
Now in his fourth decade of making pizza at his eponymous restaurant in Tonawanda, Gino Pinzone is a part of the old guard who made Buffalo pizza a thing. At seventy years old, he still gets behind the counter of Gino’s Pizza Place at 9 a.m. to make dough, prep sauce, and mentor a new generation of employees.
You’ve been a fixture in the local food scene for decades. Where did that passion for cooking begin?
Everything started back in Sicily. My mother had eleven children, so she worked at home day and night, night and day, constantly cooking for fourteen people. I’m number eight, so I did a lot of helping, making everything you could possibly make at home. I still do it for myself today. I learned everything from her.
Did she teach you to bake?
In those days, we really could not afford meat. Bread was everything. Chinese people use rice. Mexicans use tortilla shells. We were heavy on bread. When it came out of the oven, it was a treat just to put extra virgin olive oil and black pepper on it. That was it.
How did you end up owning a pizzeria?
I went to Buffalo State for Industrial Arts; I was going to be a teacher. But in 1978, my older brother opened a pizzeria and asked me and my brother Frank to work for him. I liked it a lot. I never finished my master's degree in teaching because I was doing okay making pizzas with my brother! I opened my first solo place in November 1983, and here I am today.
What do you love the most?
My employees. Some started as high school students from across the street. They start folding boxes and then, little by little, I teach them how to do a few things here and there. They might go away for college, but they always come back. It’s rewarding. Take care of the employees because the employees will always take care of you. And that’s what they do. I trust them, and they do a great job.
It sounds almost like a family atmosphere .
I get kids coming in who might be a little quiet or shy. Their parents ask if I can hire them, to get them out of their bedrooms and away from the video games. Next thing you know, they’re hopping around and working and loving it. I tell them, “You’re learning a skill.”
It’s not just about making pizzas but also learning how to get around a restaurant. You need to do dishes, you need to cut celery, you need to do this... Even if they graduate and get a degree, they can go anywhere in the world and work in a pizzeria because they know how a kitchen moves.
Many of the restaurant’s Instagram reels feature you. Do you enjoy being in the spotlight?
[Laughs] My son Phil does all that! He puts the camera in my face and says, “Dad, we’re introducing eggplant pizza today.” I always tell him, “Phil, I’m not doing a second take.” Whatever comes out of me, comes out. We did one video recently that had 20,000 viewers. People come in now just because they want to see me and talk to me.
Why have you never expanded to a second location?
I want to be totally responsible for everything that comes out of the place. I do all the prep work. I’m there from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. every day. On Fridays, I’m there until dinner is over. On Sundays, I’m there until the Bills game is over.  Nobody does it like the owner. It’s hard to train somebody to do things the way I do. Nowadays, people open five places and there’s no personal feeling.
And after forty years, most people would be taking it easy. What keeps you coming back every morning?
It’s not the money. It’s the DNA of a pizza guy in me. I see regulars who came in as kids now bringing their own grandkids in and putting them up on my counter. Why would I walk away? It makes it all worthwhile.

The cause of death for Chad Lowe and Kim Painter’s 13-year-old daughter, Fiona, who was also the niece of actor Rob Lowe, has been released.
According to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner, Fiona was pronounced dead at a hospital on Tuesday at 1:14 a.m., just weeks before what would have been her 14th birthday. The manner was ruled a suicide.
Fiona was the second-oldest child of the “Pretty Little Liars” alum and his actress wife, who also share daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, 10. The couple married in 2010, three years after Lowe’s divorce from Oscar-winner Hilary Swank.
They confirmed Fiona’s death in a statement to People on Tuesday night, describing her as “a loving young girl who was smart, creative, and loved to dance.”
“We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona,” they said.
“She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents,” the couple continued. “In fact, she was the light of our lives.”
The family concluded their statement by encouraging those “struggling with mental health” to reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline for help.
Lowe’s father, Chuck Lowe, also paid tribute to his late granddaughter on Wednesday with a post on Instagram. It featured a photo of Fiona smiling in a swimming pool.
“Rest in peace sweet Fiona,” he captioned the image.

A new generation of Hillman College students arrived on campus in Season 1 of A Different World , and soon, their education will continue. The sequel series from showrunner and executive producer Felicia Pride has officially been renewed for Season 2.
“We are beyond excited to return to Hillman and continue to tell meaningful and heartfelt stories that resonate across generations. I am thrilled for our brilliant cast and our hardworking crew,” Pride exclusively tells Tudum. “It's so validating to be bolstered by our amazing audience.”
A Different World Season 1 launched on Sept. 24 with honors, making the Netflix English TV Top 10 list. “It’s because of our incredible fans that we've received such a swift Season 2 pickup! You all have watched, rewatched, posted about, created content around, and hosted events for our show. Your support, passion, and love mean the absolute world,” Pride says. “From the passionate pleas for their favorite ’ships to feeling seen by a particular character to uncovering well-laid Easter eggs , the conversations fans have been having are so rich and joyful. And I love that audiences are watching it together — parents with children, college friends, and extended family — all enjoying it in community.”
Executive producer and director Debbie Allen can’t wait for the next chapter of A Different World . “Yay! Hallelujah! The people and Netflix have spoken. A Different World brought something everybody needed: joy, romance, relevance, authenticity, and HEART,” she says. “Thank you for getting us into the Top 10 worldwide ! And now, gear up! We’re coming back at you with Season 2!”
Looking ahead, Pride promises “more Hillman, more college life, more friendship, more romance, more Black joy, and more HBCU greatness” in A Different World Season 2. You can also expect answers to some of your most burning questions following Deborah Wayne’s (Maleah Joi Moon) first year at Hillman. “Of course, we left Season 1 with quite a few cliffhangers that we must address in Season 2,” says Pride.

articles.title_zh: Taylor T-Shirts Impact Lives Through Partnership with World Orphans
articles.content_orig:
Lydia Wilhelm 02 October 2026
Would it really be a prospective student visit without a free t-shirt? If you see a student walking backwards across campus giving a Taylor tour, you’re bound to see some visitors with classic Taylor purple t-shirts hanging over their arms. However, you might not know that this common prospective student gift is creating uncommon change in the lives of Guatemalan families through Taylor’s partnership with World Orphans .
World Orphans is a non-profit organization with a vision of relational healing and financial independence for families who have been separated due to poverty or abuse. One of the ministry arms within the organization is the World Orphans Market , an economic empowerment program. This program equips women with sewing skills, and these women are then employed as artisans to return to them the dignity of meaningful work and financial freedom. All of World Orphans’ work is grounded in a Christ-centered philosophy of human worth: everyone is created with intrinsic dignity and with a God-given purpose. Additionally, World Orphans works through local churches, ensuring that these women are supported by Christ-centered communities as they work their way out of poverty and towards better lives for their families.
Like so many Taylor stories, Taylor’s journey to partnering with World Orphans is a story of community. When the Admissions team connected with World Orphans, they saw an opportunity—an opportunity for Taylor as an organization to model the same mission it seeks to foster in its student body. Taylor always has a need for t-shirts—particularly in Admissions. Here, Taylor’s tangible need for shirts meets these Guatemalan women’s tangible need for living-wage work, creating a true, mutually beneficial partnership.
As the Admissions team collaborated with World Orphans’ Guatemalan team, they encountered some community connections that made one thing clear—God had already been opening doors for this partnership. One of these connections was Lily Sachsenmeier ’26, who finished her Orphaned & Vulnerable Children degree interning at World Orphans in Guatemala, where "a highlight was getting to talk with social workers at World Orphans who support local families, empowering parents with education and resources to care for their children. I was really moved by the personal experiences they shared and by their passion for their work."
During her time in Guatemala, Sachsenmeier also had the opportunity to meet some of the artisans making the t-shirts for Taylor Admissions, bringing this community story full circle.
Reflecting on Taylor’s choosing World Orphans to supply their next batch of Admissions t-shirts, Sachsenmeier said, "I’m deeply touched that Taylor is partnering with World Orphans. As a student, I got many free t-shirts for events and programs, and I’m so glad that Taylor is being intentional about where they source some of these t-shirts. I’m incredibly proud that Taylor is investing in t-shirts made by these women in Guatemala as part of World Orphans’ economic empowerment program!"
At Taylor, a t-shirt is so much more than a clothing item—it’s a walking billboard for who we are. It says, "I believe in what goes on here." Now, Taylor purple has additional purpose. These t-shirts are a physical manifestation of our mission to "minister Christ’s redemptive love, grace, and truth to a world in need." They are a reminder of a God who opens doors. And a reminder of what a true partnership can look like.

articles.title_orig: Apple is reportedly building a smart home camera that won't record video footage of you or anyone else
articles.title_zh: Apple is reportedly building a smart home camera that won't record video footage of you or anyone else
articles.content_orig:
The device will apparently use AI to analyze activity in your home without actually filming it.
After finally making Siri a half-decent assistant in this year's round of major OS updates, it looks like the smart home is going to Apple's big area of focus in the coming months. Reliable Apple insider Mark Gurman revealed earlier this week that the company's long-awaited home hub could arrive later in October, and in the debut episode of his new Power On podcast, he predicted that a security camera may follow. But unlike its many soon-to-be rivals, this one somewhat bizarrely won't actually record video.
As well as the home hub device, which will be the centrepiece of the whole Siri-led smart home push, Gurman claims that Apple will also launch more powerful versions of the HomePod mini and Apple TV, which will both support the new Siri AI ecosystem. But the camera is arguably more interesting, as much for what it can't do as what it can.
The Bloomberg reporter says the camera device is a companion product to Apple's also as-yet unannounced smart home display, which the company is referring to internally as J490. These small cameras can be installed around your home and will apparently be cylindrical, resembling chapstick. Gurman says they will have a very low frame rate and crucially won't actually offer video recording as a feature.
What's the point of a camera that doesn't capture moving images, you may ask? Apple appears to be mindful of the growing and very reasonable concerns about over-surveillance and what happens with that data, and so the sensor will instead use AI to analyze movement in your home. It's not clear if you'll be able to pull still images from it, but it will be able to do facial recognition.
If the camera identifies someone walking into a room, it can notify you of whether you know that person or not, but you'll only receive text descriptions. As Gurman points out, a total lack of video footage probably won't be particularly helpful to the police in the event that someone breaks into your home, but the added layer of privacy would definitely make Apple's camera stand out in a crowded market.
Gurman added that the security camera will use "a very similar technology to what they're going to be using for the AirPods with cameras," which leaked over the summer. Based on code buried in an early build of macOS Tahoe 26.7, these AirPods will each have their own tiny embedded cameras that take extremely low resolution RGB still images that can be analyzed using Visual Intelligence. In the wake of Meta's "pervert glasses" fallout, Apple's camera-equipped AirPods reportedly won't be able to take pictures or record video.

articles.title_orig: BU Welcomes Inaugural Class of Davis United World College Scholars
articles.title_zh: BU Welcomes Inaugural Class of Davis United World College Scholars
articles.content_orig:
BU’s inaugural group of Davis Scholars–international students from select high schools–will gather periodically throughout the year to share experiences and insights.
Boston University welcomed 37 international freshmen this fall as its first Davis United World College Scholars . Based at Vermont’s Middlebury College, Davis UWC is the largest source of financial aid for international undergraduates in the United States, awarding scholarships to graduates of 18 designated high schools across the globe. BU President Melissa Gilliam arranged BU’s admission to Davis’s participating network of 100-plus American colleges and universities.
The scholarships cover students’ full, demonstrated need for the cost of attending BU: tuition, housing, and fees. (Financial needs vary by student, but most require aid to cover the full attendance cost.) This year’s inaugural cohort represents 22 nations enrolled in seven BU schools and colleges. The goal is to grow the program to 80 enrolled scholars by the end of the second year.
Each scholar has a faculty or staff mentor assigned to them for their undergraduate years, and each mentor in turn advises a small group of Davis Scholars, bringing them together once a month in addition to individual meetings. Mentors will connect students with academics and experiential learning aligned with their interests. All scholars will gather several times throughout the year for special events, including faculty dinners and a Boston cultural outing. Overseeing the implementation of the program throughout the year are Laura Johnson, senior assistant provost for undergraduate affairs, and Anne Corriveau, director of international admissions.
Before coming to BU, Gilliam’s roles at the University of Chicago included chief of family planning and contraceptive research. “I saw firsthand the incredible talent, maturity, and global awareness Davis Scholars brought to that campus,” she wrote in her Davis UWC admission request. “Similar to your program’s five pillars, global engagement is a key element of BU’s DNA and a necessary component to our University’s and our students’ ability to have a positive impact across the world. BU has a long and rich history of being a global university and for enrolling international students.”
Davis Scholarships are “an extraordinary complement to Boston University’s commitment to making a world-class education accessible to talented students from around the globe,” says Kelly Walter, BU associate vice president for enrollment and dean of admissions.
BU Today spoke with two of BU’s inaugural Davis Scholars—both enrolled at the Questrom School of Business—who shared their stories and hopes for their time at the University.
“Yasmine, you’re really outspoken,” a friend once told Gerverk, who doesn’t argue the point. At her school in the Norwegian city of Moss, whenever a teacher asked a question and waited for someone’s hand to go up, “normally, it was me. I’ll take one for the class,” Geverk says. That outspokenness so impressed peers that they admitted her to the youth municipal council, an advisory group to the city government on youth perspectives, at the record-young age of 13. She ultimately served on Norway’s arm of the European Youth Parliament.
Her personal story—daughter of a Kurdish Iranian engineer and a Norwegian teacher, growing up in an immigrant neighborhood of Moss, going abroad to attend an internationally diverse UWC high school in the Netherlands—reinforced her desire to attend BU with its international student body and to participate in the Davis UWC program.
“I’ve kind of lived between cultures,” Geverk says, “a Norwegian culture and the Kurdish, Middle Eastern culture.” She roomed at her Dutch high school with students from Ukraine, China, the Netherlands, Oman, Georgia, and Bhutan. “One of the main reasons I applied to Davis United World Colleges is because I knew I would meet people from all over the world. That’s also why I wanted to pursue studying at a school that was really priding itself on being international.”
Post-graduation, Geverk plans to pursue a career in business. While she might get involved with student government at BU, she’s also interested in such activities as Innovate@BU and Questrom’s Entrepreneurship Club .
“Most likely, not having the Davis Scholarship would mean that I would have to go back home for university, or to another Scandinavian country” where higher education is less expensive than in the US, she explains. “That wasn’t something that I wanted. I wanted to go out and explore more. So without Davis, I would not be able to do that. And I feel like I wouldn’t get this level of an education without Davis.”
Geverk is determined to take advantage of all that Boston University has to offer—both in the classroom and beyond. “You lose 100 percent of the shots you don’t take,” she says.
Silja (she’s asked that her last name not be used for privacy reasons) co-led a “Human Library”—a periodic gathering during the school year in which students shared stories, some personal (identity, family conflicts, religious or cultural upbringing), others global—at her Finnish high school . “We wanted to create an environment,” she says, “where students practiced listening not necessarily with the intent of agreeing, but with the intent of understanding.” The library’s student leaders worked with speakers before each session to help them develop and share their stories.
“On the day of the event, we decorated our school library with warm lights, pillows, and candles to give the space an intimate feel,” she says. “It made me realize how easy it is to judge another individual based on our own upbringing and the values that were shaped by our surroundings. I often found myself wondering that, if I had grown up where the person I disagree with did, surrounded by the same experiences, fears and values they had, how differently might I see the world?”
Silja is exploring how she could start a similar initiative at BU, including the use of social media to share stories to reach busy students at this vast institution. She’s also looking for existing student groups touching on her passions, which include business and international relations. “I’m still very new to BU, so I’m trying to leave room to discover things I might not have expected to be interested in.”
A double major in business and international relations, she was looking at US and European colleges before BU and the Davis scholarship beckoned: “BU ultimately offered most of what I was looking for: a large and diverse student body, a vibrant urban campus, and the opportunity to pursue my interests in both business and international relations. I think the Davis program is a wonderful way to continue the UWC experience beyond high school by bringing students to universities across the US. I love that the Davis network allows that community to extend beyond UWC itself, which makes the program especially meaningful to me.
“Coming to university in a new country can be intimidating, so there is something really comforting about knowing that there is already a wider UWC community here.”
“What distinguishes the Davis Program is that it is about much more than financial support,” says Walter. “It invests in students who have already demonstrated an extraordinary commitment to cross-cultural understanding, leadership, service, and academic excellence through the United World Colleges movement.”

Tip Toe refuses to be misunderstood. Premiering Oct. 2 on Starz, the British miniseries from Queer as Folk creator and Doctor Who reviver Russell T Davies set its stakes as high as the lamppost from which Alan Cumming ’s character is seen hanging, dead, just outside his home, in the very first scene. Reminders of this awful outcome open each episode, preceding flashbacks that take us through the escalation of tensions between Cumming’s Leo Struthers and his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), over the course of just 10 days. Scripty speechifying and a finale that strains believability notwithstanding, Tip Toe is, in its unabashed melodrama, a harrowing cri de coeur about masculinity in crisis and queer liberation reversed.
Leo and Clive have a few things in common. Both pushing 60, the men have been sharing a wall in outwardly identical Manchester rowhouses for 14 years. They’ve also both, when we meet them, hit rough patches in life. Clive, an electrician, is having trouble finding enough work to support a family that includes touchy 16-year-old George (Jackson Connor) and 25-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans), who assists his dad on jobs but isn’t exactly earning the kind of money that would enable him to move out. As gossip swirls that he’s cheated on her, Clive’s wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), constantly berates him. Meanwhile, Leo’s longtime partner, Curtis (Charlie Condou), has left him for a woman. Not only is he unmoored in his personal life, overrelying on his indulgent best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington); he’s also struggling to manage Spit & Polish, the bar in Manchester’s gay nightlife district that he and Curtis used to run together.
Alan Cumming in Tip Toe Starz
Early one morning, Leo chases after an anonymous hookup who has just absconded with his laptop—only to find himself locked out of his house in his underwear. Clive reluctantly lets him in to call Stephanie for a spare key, making clear all the while that Leo’s lifestyle disgusts him and that he’s uncomfortable having his neighbor around his sons, one underage and the other a musclebound Adonis. The thing is, Clive’s kids are nowhere near as innocent as he thinks. And he’s drawn further out of his comfort zone when Leo, against his better judgment, hires Clive and Saul to fix some wiring at Spit & Polish. The first sign of worlds perilously colliding is when a bar employee recognizes Saul from OnlyFans . An unsubtle but rhetorically effective montage of Leo and the Gosses, each in separate rooms, indulging in their preferred forms of pornography, reveals both the secrets they’re keeping from each other and the loneliness they share.
While Tip Toe spends time with all of these characters, Leo is its protagonist. And he’s an admirably imperfect one, charming and fundamentally kind but also pugnacious, prone to exaggeration, self-centered enough to earn Stephanie’s accusation that he doesn’t really value women. (She, in turn, shows glimpses of the J.K. Rowling-style transphobia that seems to afflict British feminists more than most.) His bar functions as a portal into the lives of less privileged members of the queer and trans communities, from his old, flamboyant, gender-nonconforming friend and unrequited admirer, Melba (Paul Rhys), to a 20-something trans bartender (Iz Hesketh), who’s calling herself Zee as she deliberates on a permanent female name—and who dodges transphobic violence daily. The question of whether the visibility Leo’s generation fought so hard to win has backfired, making them all easy targets, haunts the series.
David Morrissey in Tip Toe Starz
Davies recently raged against the homophobia of the early AIDS crisis in the searing period piece It’s a Sin and looked queasily ahead to a dystopian future in the sci-fi family drama Years & Years . Tip Toe unites their themes to complete a sort of trilogy, combining the anxieties of LGBTQ people, intrafamilial alienation, economic strife, the social-media panopticon, and an overarching sense of doom into a fire sermon against our toxic present. That it shares its Manchester setting with the far breezier, Y2K-era Queer as Folk underlines just how much that community’s outlook has changed in a quarter-century. And the fact that Cumming’s phenomenal performance is airing concurrently in the U.S. with The Traitors: New Blood , which he hosts with high-camp aplomb and an androgynous glam wardrobe, highlights the cognitive dissonance of a society where queerness is embraced—by everyone except the sizable faction that actively hates it. More than just Leo’s antagonist, Clive is an avatar for straight masculinity in crisis, desperately vulnerable but too terrified of showing emotion to say so. Morrissey captures that tightness of that bind. Devalued at home and work, he dabbles in conspiracy theories and marinates in videos of “real deaths.” His story can feel like an adult Adolescence .
Tip Toe also calls to mind other recent series ( BEEF , too many reality shows about feuding neighbors) and films ( Eddington , Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri ) that translate current political and social fault lines into tête-à-tête conflicts. On both sides of the Atlantic, storytellers are trying to understand the hateful tenor of the contemporary public sphere by distilling it down to its simplest, me-against-you form. The difference here is that, although Leo and other characters are shown to have healthy senses of humor, Tip Toe itself doesn’t share those titles’ tone of black-comic absurdity. It isn’t a funny show. Sometimes its seriousness veers into stridency. I didn’t find the abrupt escalation to Leo’s death particularly convincing.
Yet, as in It’s a Sin and Years & Years , it’s the incandescent clarity of Davies’ anger and fear that make Tip Toe powerful. For all the dumbed-down dialogue we get from streamers worried they’ll lose distracted viewers unless someone on screen recaps the plot every five minutes, it’s rare to hear characters plainly state things like: “History tells us one thing—that blood and fire and retribution always happen. And right now it’s coming for us.” When Stephanie confesses her worry that she’ll die in 30 years without living to see the pendulum of progress swing society out of what she calls a “new Dark Age,” I suspect she’s speaking for a lot of people. Too often in fiction (which this is, despite ending title cards that purport to update us on the characters’ lives post-Leo), social commentary is inoculated with optimism or couched in irony. In its unblinking earnestness, Tip Toe ’s melodrama accesses a truth that transcends any shortcomings of its plot.

articles.title_zh: The 1893 World's Fair Is the Subject of a New 'Chicago Stories' Documentary
articles.content_orig:
“This fair not only changed Chicago, it shaped the American imagination,” says Peter Marks, one of the producers and writers of the new documentary The World’s Fair of 1893 , which leads off a new season of our Chicago Stories on Friday, October 2 at 8:00 pm and at wttw.com/chicagostories . Walt Disney’s father was a carpenter who helped build the fair, while the illustrations of the Emerald City in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum, who attended, look “an awful lot like the White City” of the fair. The World’s Columbian Exposition not only inspired people; it also showed the world a new Chicago and introduced Vienna Beef, the zipper, and much more.
We spoke to Marks, his fellow producer and writer Tania Lindsay, and digital producer Meredith Francis about the fair, the documentary, and the companion website.
The Guide: Why is this World’s Fair so important to Chicago?
Peter Marks: This is the moment Chicago announced itself to the world. Only 20 years after the Great Fire , Chicago had transformed into an economic powerhouse and the birthplace of the skyscraper. [The skyscraper is the subject of another new Chicago Stories .] But people, especially New Yorkers, still dismissed us as a smelly ‘cow town.’ When Chicago beat out New York for the right to host the World’s Fair, Daniel Burnham and John Root had less than three years to turn a swamp in Jackson Park into a city that would dazzle and delight the world. Twenty-seven million visitors later, nobody could call Chicago a cow town anymore.
Tania Lindsay: It put the city on the map as a rival to New York and Paris. It also physically reshaped the city and seeded institutions, ideas, and products we still use daily.
The Guide: Why revisit the World’s Fair now?
Lindsay: Partly because there is no bad time to revisit the wonder that was the White City. And partly to remind Chicago of something about itself: That this is a city with a long history of doing hard and wonderful things, if imperfectly, and showing the world that we are much more than whatever the news says in any given year. The imperfect part matters too, and while we celebrate all the glorious wonders of the fair, the film doesn’t skip the hard parts, like who got left out, who got taken advantage of – or worse – and who carried on despite tragedy.
Marks: I think there’s something valuable about remembering a moment when Chicago took on the impossible. The fair is a reminder of Chicago’s “I Will” spirit, and what we can accomplish when we think big.
The Guide: How did you try to take a new approach towards a topic many Chicagoans already know?
Marks: One of the things we wanted to do was separate H.H. Holmes the murderer from H.H. Holmes the myth. Many people have read The Devil in the White City , in which Holmes builds this elaborate murder castle to lure unsuspecting victims. But that isn’t quite what happened. Newspaper reporters exaggerated the details, publishing fabricated diagrams of secret chambers and a crematory.
Meredith Francis: Another darker story to come out of the fair was the assassination of Chicago's mayor, Carter Harrison, just a couple days before the fair was set to close.
The Guide: What is something new that you learned in making this documentary?
Lindsay: Brownies can be highly controversial. While Bertha Palmer’s kitchen at the Palmer House Hotel is given credit as inventor of the beloved brownie, others question whether that apricot-glazed confection should be considered a brownie at all. It’s a highly sensitive topic. Some historians refused to comment, others cautiously avoided picking a side. Some said one thing off the record, and something different on. We may never know the right answer. But we’ll always have brownies.
The Guide: What’s something that most Chicagoans don’t know about the fair?
Marks: Most Chicagoans think the World’s Fair vanished, but it didn’t. If you walk down the Midway Plaisance at the University of Chicago, that’s where belly dancers once strutted and the first Ferris wheel spun. The Museum of Science and Industry was originally the Palace of Fine Arts. The Art Institute was created for the fair. There’s a ticket booth tucked in the yard of a private residence. The Obama Presidential Library rises on ground where the Horticulture and Women’s Building once stood. The fair is still very much around us if you know where to look.
Francis: On the companion website, we want people to be able to immerse themselves in this world, and to be able to imagine what it might have been like to attend the fair. We have some amazing historical images that go beyond the typical picture people might have in their heads. Our talented graphics team has created a really cool 3D imagining of what it would have been like to walk through the fair. It gives you a sense of just how expansive it was, and what it took to achieve that.
The Guide: What’s your favorite lasting impact of the fair?
Marks: For me, it’s Daniel Burnham’s vision. The White City helped inspire the City Beautiful movement and Burnham’s 1909 Plan of Chicago . There are times our skyline, parks, and museums still take my breath away.
Francis: There are a couple things that I would argue have made my life better: An early model of the modern dishwasher (invented by a woman!), and the brownie.
Lindsay: My favorite may well be the Ferris Wheel. I love that it exists because Chicago had a serious case of envy and wanted to top Paris’s 1889 World’s Fair stunner, the Eiffel Tower. George Ferris engineered the first-of-its-kind, giant wheel, with riding cars the size of city buses. It was a sensation when it debuted on the Midway Plaisance, which helped become the blueprint for the modern amusement park . Every time I see the wheel at Navy Pier, I see part of the Fair’s legacy, still spinning today.
